domains.name: Active Directory & Identity Defense
domains.summary: How Active Directory works, how attackers abuse it, and how defenders harden it — from trust design to tiered administration and phishing-resistant authentication.

scenarios.title: Trust Falls Downhill
scenarios.situation: Your company acquires a smaller firm and creates a two-way forest trust between the two AD forests so users can access resources in both. A colleague says 'it's just like a VPN tunnel between the forests.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the most important thing to understand about that trust before relying on it?
choices: A forest trust is an authentication path, not a network tunnel — and in a two-way trust, compromise can flow either direction, so both forests' security postures matter.
The trust encrypts all traffic between the forests automatically.
The trust merges both forests into one domain.
Trusts are one-way by definition and cannot be reversed.
scenarios.why: A trust says 'I will honor your authentication decisions.' A two-way trust means both sides say it, so the security of each forest now depends on the other — a compromised admin in the acquired forest can authenticate into your resources. That is why trust design is a security decision first and a convenience decision second.
scenarios.hint: Who is really being trusted here — the network, or the other forest's administrators?
objectives: AD structure and trust: trust relationships

scenarios.title: The Schema Master Is Down
scenarios.situation: During a maintenance window the domain controller holding the Schema Master FSMO role is powered off for hardware replacement. Help desk asks whether anyone can install applications or change passwords until it returns.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct answer?
choices: Normal operations continue — password changes and logons are handled by other DCs. Only schema modifications (like extending the schema for a new application) are blocked until the role holder returns.
Nothing works until the Schema Master is back; all authentication stops.
All five FSMO roles move automatically to another DC within minutes.
Users must be told to stop logging in until the DC is restored.
scenarios.why: FSMO roles are single-master operations for tasks that cannot safely happen on two DCs at once. The Schema Master only gates schema changes — a rare operation. Day-to-day work (logons, password changes, group membership) is multi-master and unaffected. Knowing which role gates which operation is the core FSMO skill; the five roles are Schema Master, Domain Naming Master, PDC Emulator, RID Master, and Infrastructure Master.
scenarios.hint: Ask what the Schema Master actually does day-to-day — and what it only does once in a blue moon.
objectives: AD structure and trust: FSMO roles

scenarios.title: Service Account With an SPN and a Weak Password
scenarios.situation: A vulnerability scan flags a service account that has a Service Principal Name registered and a password that has not changed in six years. The account runs a legacy reporting tool nobody wants to touch.
scenarios.prompt: Why is this combination specifically dangerous?
choices: Any domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket (TGS) for that SPN and then crack it offline — Kerberoasting. The old password is the weak link, and the attack needs no privileges and leaves little noise.
Service accounts cannot be attacked because they are not interactive logons.
The danger is only theoretical; Kerberos tickets cannot be cracked offline.
The fix is to delete the SPN so the service stops working entirely.
scenarios.why: Kerberoasting works because TGS tickets are encrypted with the service account's password hash, and any authenticated user may request them. The attacker takes the ticket home and guesses the password offline — no lockouts, no alerts. Long-lived, weak service-account passwords plus SPNs are the classic setup. Defenses: long random passwords (managed service accounts rotate them automatically) and monitoring for unusual TGS requests.
scenarios.hint: What does the attacker walk away with, and what do they need it to decrypt?

scenarios.title: Pre-Auth Disabled 'For Compatibility'
scenarios.situation: An audit finds three user accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled — set years ago 'for compatibility' with an old application that is long gone. The accounts have normal user privileges.
scenarios.prompt: What attack does this enable, and what is the fix?
choices: AS-REP roasting: without pre-authentication, anyone can request the account's AS-REP response and crack it offline, no credentials required. Re-enable pre-authentication (the default) and rotate the passwords.
Nothing — pre-authentication is optional and disabling it is harmless.
It enables pass-the-hash, which is fixed by changing the domain functional level.
The accounts must be deleted; they can never be secured.
scenarios.why: Kerberos pre-authentication proves the requester knows the password before the KDC answers. With it disabled, the KDC hands out an encrypted AS-REP to literally anyone who asks for that username — and that blob is crackable offline. It is one of the cheapest account takeovers in AD: no privileges needed, just a username list. The fix is a checkbox (re-enable pre-auth) plus a password rotation.
scenarios.hint: What is the KDC giving away for free here, and to whom?

scenarios.title: The Help Desk Admin Problem
scenarios.situation: Your organization has 40 help desk staff who all hold Domain Admin 'because they sometimes need to reset things.' A tiered-administration proposal suggests Tier 0 (domain controllers, identity systems), Tier 1 (servers), and Tier 2 (workstations), with separate privileged accounts per tier.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the tiered model matter, and what is the first concrete change?
choices: It stops credential theft from spreading: an admin's credentials are only ever exposed on systems at their tier, so a compromised workstation cannot yield Domain Admin hashes. First change: remove standing Domain Admin from help desk and issue tier-appropriate accounts.
It is just paperwork; 40 Domain Admins is fine if they are trustworthy.
The first change should be renaming the Administrator account.
Tiering only matters for compliance audits, not real security.
scenarios.why: Pass-the-hash and token theft mean that wherever an admin logs on, their credentials become stealable on that machine. Forty Domain Admins logging into workstations means Domain Admin material sits on forty attack surfaces. Tiering enforces a simple rule: Tier 0 credentials never touch Tier 1 or Tier 2 systems. LAPS (unique local admin passwords per machine) and Credential Guard then shrink what is stealable at each tier.
scenarios.hint: If an attacker owns one help desk workstation today, what do they walk away with under the current model?
objectives: Hardening: tiered admin model, LAPS, Credential Guard

scenarios.title: DCSync From a 'Backup' Account
scenarios.situation: A routine review finds a service account with the 'Replicating Directory Changes All' permission on the domain — granted years ago to a backup product that was replaced. The account is still active.
scenarios.prompt: What is the risk, and what is the correct remediation?
choices: That permission lets the account impersonate a domain controller and pull password hashes via replication — the DCSync technique. Remove the permission (and the stale account), then audit who else holds replication rights.
It is harmless; replication permissions are read-only and cannot expose credentials.
The risk is only that backups fail; re-grant the permission to be safe.
DCSync requires Domain Admin, so a service account cannot perform it.
scenarios.why: DCSync abuses a legitimate replication right: ask the DC for changes 'as if' you were another DC, and it hands over hashes — including the krbtgt account's, which enables golden-ticket forgery. The permission is powerful by design and should exist on almost nothing. Stale grants to dead products are how attackers inherit domain-replication rights without ever touching an admin account. Audit replication rights regularly and treat any unexpected holder as an incident.
scenarios.hint: What is the account allowed to pretend to be, and what does a domain controller hand to its peers?

scenarios.title: The Scope Question
scenarios.situation: EDR flags Mimikatz on one workstation. The user is a standard user with no admin rights.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct scoping response?
choices: Assume lateral movement until ruled out: isolate the host, hunt for the initial access vector and any credential material the host touched, review privileged logons from that host — one workstation is the starting point, not the boundary.
Reimage the workstation and close the ticket.
The user has no admin rights, so impact is minimal.
Run antivirus and monitor.
scenarios.why: The correct approach scopes aggressively: Mimikatz on any host means credential theft was attempted, and the host's network position (not the user's rights) defines the blast radius. Reimaging destroys forensics.
scenarios.hint: What did the attacker touch from that host?
evidence: Helpdesk admin logged on WS-118 yesterday

scenarios.title: The 2 AM Call
scenarios.situation: Confirmed DCSync from a compromised server at 2 AM. You must wake leadership.
scenarios.prompt: What do you communicate in the first call?
choices: Situation, impact, actions underway, decisions needed, next update time: 'DCSync indicates full domain compromise; isolating now; need authorization for krbtgt rotation; next update 03:00.' Facts, not theories; decisions, not details.
Full technical breakdown of DCSync.
Wait until morning with complete information.
'Everything is fine, we are handling it.'
scenarios.why: The correct approach gives leadership what they need for decisions: scope, actions, and the specific authorization required. Technical depth comes in the written follow-up.
scenarios.hint: What decision can only leadership make right now?
evidence: 02:17; leadership asleep; krbtgt rotation needs authorization

domains.name: AdFind & Active Directory Reconnaissance Hunting
domains.summary: How ransomware operators map Active Directory with the free AdFind query tool — and how defenders detect the recon, hunt it with behavior-based logic, and use its artifacts to rebuild the intrusion timeline.

scenarios.title: The recon that wore a helpdesk badge
scenarios.situation: Tuesday 09:14. Your EDR fires on WKSTN-214 in accounting: adfind.exe executed by marisol.vega, a standard user with no admin rights. The parent process is cmd.exe launched from a batch file. Command line: adfind -f (objectcategory=computer) -sc computers_pwdnotreqd > C:\Windows\Temp\c.txt. Marisol says she was ‘running a script IT sent her.’
scenarios.prompt: What is your triage call?
evidence:
adfind.exe | parent: cmd.exe (recon.bat)
user: marisol.vega (standard, non-admin)
cmdline: adfind -f (objectcategory=computer) -sc computers_pwdnotreqd > C:\Windows\Temp\c.txt
Marisol has no admin duties. No change ticket references recon.bat. Two more adfind runs followed within 90 seconds: (objectcategory=person), then trustdmp.
choices: Close as benign: AdFind is a legitimate admin tool and Marisol says IT sent the script.
Escalate as suspected ransomware reconnaissance: non-admin user, batch wrapper, burst of discovery queries with output staged to Temp.
Block the adfind.exe hash enterprise-wide and close the alert.
Reimage the workstation immediately without further investigation.
scenarios.why: AdFind is dual-use: legitimate for admins, but a ransomware-affiliate recon staple. The discriminating facts are context, not the binary — a non-admin user, a batch wrapper, a burst of discovery queries (computers, people, trusts), and output staged to Temp. That pattern matches pre-ransomware AD mapping. Blocking the hash alone is theater, since the tool is trivially renamed, and reimaging destroys the forensic artifacts (those Temp output files) that anchor your timeline.
scenarios.hint: Ask what separates an admin's AdFind from an attacker's: who ran it, from where, how many queries, and where the output went.

scenarios.title: Three queries in ninety seconds
scenarios.situation: You are writing the detection for AdFind abuse. The SOC is drowning in noise: your first draft fired on every domain admin who ever ran the tool. You need logic that catches ransomware-affiliate recon while letting legitimate administration through.
scenarios.prompt: Which detection design is most defensible?
evidence:
A: any adfind.exe execution
B: 3+ distinct recon tokens (objectcategory=person/computer, trustdmp, dcmodes, computers_pwdnotreqd, ‘Domain Admins’) with output redirect (>) inside 2 minutes
C: adfind.exe only on domain controllers
D: command lines containing the word ‘trust’
choices: A: alert on any adfind.exe execution — simplest, catches everything.
B: burst of distinct recon query types plus output redirection in a short window, on hosts where the user is not a known admin — behavior over filename.
C: only monitor domain controllers — that is where AD lives.
D: match the substring ‘trust’ — trusts are the attacker’s real goal.
scenarios.why: Behavior beats filename: attackers rename binaries freely, so hash and name matching is brittle. The published hunting logic (Microsoft’s Defender query, Sigma’s win_susp_adfind) keys on distinctive command-line tokens — objectcategory filters, trustdmp, dcmodes, computers_pwdnotreqd — combined with output redirection and a burst threshold, scoped to unexpected users and hosts. That is what separates a ransomware affiliate’s recon batch from a domain admin’s one-off query, and it survives renaming.
scenarios.hint: What survives when the attacker renames adfind.exe to svchost.exe?

scenarios.title: The timestamps that moved the breach
scenarios.situation: During scoping you find C:\Windows\Temp\ad1.txt, ad2.txt, ad3.txt on a file server — AdFind outputs enumerating users, computers, and trusts. Their creation timestamps are 11 days older than your assumed initial-access date. Legal is drafting the breach notification on the old timeline.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do with these files?
evidence:
ad1.txt (users) — created 11 days before assumed initial access
ad2.txt (computers) — same day, 4 minutes later
ad3.txt (trusts) — same day, 9 minutes later
Initial access was estimated from the first EDR alert. No earlier evidence was found — until these files.
choices: Ignore them: text files in Temp are junk, and the EDR alert is the authoritative start.
Treat the AdFind output timestamps as the earliest hard evidence of recon, extend the intrusion window back 11 days, and tell legal the notification scope and deadlines may change.
Delete them to keep the timeline clean for the report.
Attribute them to a penetration test without checking for an engagement record.
scenarios.why: Recon output files are timeline anchors: they prove an attacker-controlled process was enumerating the domain on that date. Practitioners note these Temp-staged AdFind outputs are often the earliest hard evidence that recon began — which can push the whole intrusion timeline back. That changes dwell-time math, the scope of log review, and potentially breach-notification deadlines. Deleting them would be destruction of evidence; assuming a pen test without a record is wishful thinking.
scenarios.hint: What does a file creation timestamp prove that an alert timestamp doesn’t?

scenarios.title: Map the batch to ATT&CK
scenarios.situation: You recover the attacker’s recon batch file. It runs four AdFind passes: (objectcategory=person), (objectcategory=computer), -sc trustdmp, and a subnet enumeration. Your detection coverage map needs the ATT&CK techniques.
scenarios.prompt: Which mapping is correct?
choices: All four are T1087 Account Discovery — discovery is discovery.
T1087.002 Domain Account, T1018 Remote System Discovery, T1482 Domain Trust Discovery, T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery.
T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application for all four — they came from the internet.
T1003 Credential Dumping — enumeration is a form of dumping.
scenarios.why: ATT&CK discovery techniques split by what is being discovered: domain accounts (T1087.002), remote systems (T1018), domain trusts (T1482), and network configuration (T1016). Mapping precisely matters because coverage maps, hunt hypotheses, and Sigma rules key off technique IDs — lumping everything under one ID hides gaps. T1190 is initial access, not discovery; T1003 is credential theft, a different tactic entirely.
scenarios.hint: Discovery techniques are named for the thing discovered. What four different things did the batch enumerate?

scenarios.title: Legit or lateral?
scenarios.situation: Two AdFind executions, same week. Case A: a domain admin runs AdFind from the admin jump host during a change window to audit stale computer accounts. Case B: a service-desk user runs it at 2:14 AM from a workstation, parented by a batch file, output to Temp. Same binary, same query syntax.
scenarios.prompt: Which contextual signals decide the triage?
choices: The binary hash — if it matches the known-good AdFind, both are benign.
Context: account privilege, host role, parent process, time of day, and output destination. Case B’s combination is the attacker pattern; Case A is administration.
The query syntax — attackers use different LDAP filters than admins.
Neither can be judged; AdFind is too common to triage.
scenarios.why: Dual-use tools are judged by context, not by binary. The hash is identical in both cases — it is the same legitimate tool. What differs is who ran it (privileged admin vs standard user), from where (jump host vs workstation), how (interactive audit vs batch wrapper at 2 AM), and where the output went. Train the SOC on that five-signal checklist and AdFind stops being either ‘always fine’ or ‘always evil’.
scenarios.hint: The binary is identical in both cases. So what isn’t?

scenarios.title: After the recon
scenarios.situation: AdFind reconnaissance is confirmed on a domain-joined host: users, computers, and trusts were enumerated six hours ago. No lateral movement alerts yet. The helpdesk wants to ‘just delete the tool and move on.’
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct immediate response?
choices: Delete adfind.exe from the host and close the ticket — tool removed, problem solved.
Isolate the host, preserve the Temp output files, hunt for lateral movement (PsExec, RDP, WMI), and scope which credentials and trusts the recon exposed — recon is the precursor, not the incident.
Force a password reset for every user in the domain immediately.
Wait for the ransomware to detonate so you have a confirmed incident.
scenarios.why: Recon is the precursor to lateral movement, not the whole incident: deleting the tool removes nothing the attacker needs (they can bring it back in seconds) and destroys your evidence. The correct sequence is isolate to stop the clock, preserve the recon outputs for timeline and scoping, then hunt the techniques that follow discovery — remote execution and lateral movement — because ransomware affiliates enumerate precisely so they can move next. Domain-wide password resets before scoping are disruptive theater; waiting for detonation is negligence.
scenarios.hint: Recon answers the attacker’s question ‘what can I reach next?’ — what do you do about the answer?

scenarios.title: The Graph Lights Up
scenarios.situation: BloodHound shows a 2-hop path: Helpdesk user -> GenericAll on IT-Admins -> member of Domain Admins.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix priority and method?
choices: Critical: remove the GenericAll ACE (the choke point) immediately, then audit how it was granted and review all similar ACEs — one ACL edit closes this entire path.
Remove the user from Helpdesk.
Monitor the path but leave it — it might be needed.
Rebuild the domain.
scenarios.why: The correct approach fixes the edge, not the node: removing one ACE closes the path for everyone. The audit prevents recurrence; rebuilding is disproportionate.
scenarios.hint: What is the minimum change that closes the maximum paths?
evidence: ACE granted 2 years ago, no ticket

scenarios.title: The Enumeration Storm
scenarios.situation: A single host generates 50,000 LDAP queries in 10 minutes at 3 AM.
scenarios.prompt: What is the response?
choices: Isolate and investigate as active recon: identify the process/user, check for BloodHound/ADFind signatures, hunt for follow-on exploitation — bulk off-hours enumeration is attack preparation.
The vulnerability scanner runs at 3 AM — normal.
Block LDAP at the firewall.
Increase DC resources to handle the load.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats the pattern as hostile until proven otherwise: verify against the scanner schedule; if no match, it is recon. Blocking LDAP breaks AD; adding resources feeds the attacker.
scenarios.hint: What legitimate workload does this at 3 AM?
evidence: No scan scheduled; asset is a workstation

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Active Directory Defense as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Active Directory & Identity Defense Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Active Directory & Identity Defense is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Active Directory & Identity Defense?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Active Directory & Identity Defense issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Active Directory & Identity Defense is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Active Directory & Identity Defense supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Active Directory & Identity Defense failure in Active Directory Defense.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Active Directory & Identity Defense
evidence: All Active Directory & Identity Defense components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Navigate the Bootcamp
scenarios.situation: You have 30 days before your assessment. You open the bootcamp and see 15 domains, a terminal, drills, and a mock. You feel overwhelmed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage first week plan?
choices: Complete Start Here, then work the first three core domains in order — lessons with knowledge checks, then their scenarios, then one lab. Establish the daily loop before widening.
Take the full mock on day one to 'see where you stand,' then study randomly.
Read every lesson in all 15 domains first, then attempt scenarios in week three.
Skip lessons entirely and grind drills — speed matters more than understanding.
scenarios.why: The correct approach is the structured loop: Start Here orients you, then sequential domains build the foundation scenarios assume. The mock on day one wastes your only baseline and demoralizes; random study leaves gaps the assessment will find. Drills without understanding produce fast wrong answers.
scenarios.hint: Think about what the scenarios assume you already know.
evidence: 30 days available, ~2 hours per day on weekdays

scenarios.title: When You Get Stuck
scenarios.situation: You have failed the same scenario three times. The explanation makes sense when you read it, but you keep choosing wrong under time pressure.
scenarios.prompt: What should you do?
choices: Drop back to the lesson: re-read the concepts, write out the decision process in your own words, then re-attempt the scenario untimed before going timed again.
Keep re-attempting the scenario until you memorize the right answer.
Skip it and move on — one scenario will not decide the assessment.
Look up the answer online and move faster through the rest.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats repeated failure as a signal: the mental model is broken, not the memory. Rebuilding from the lesson concepts — in your own words — repairs the model. Memorizing the answer passes one scenario and fails the next variation. The assessment tests patterns, not instances.
scenarios.hint: Is the problem memory or the underlying mental model?
objectives: Repair mental models from lesson concepts
evidence: Scenario failed 3x: same wrong choice twice, different wrong choice once

domains.name: Kerberos Authentication Security

scenarios.title: The 8 AM Lockout Wave
scenarios.situation: Monday 8:00 AM: 300 users cannot log in — 'username or password is incorrect.' Passwords are correct. DCs online, DNS resolves.
scenarios.prompt: Where do you look first, and why?
choices: Check time sync: Kerberos allows 5-min skew, so PDC emulator drift breaks all pre-auth at once — verify w32tm and check for clock-skew failures in the DC log.
Force password resets for all 300 users.
Reboot all domain controllers.
Check firewall for port 88 blocks.
scenarios.why: The correct approach starts with the Kerberos dependency chain: every ticket is time-bound and the domain trusts the PDC emulator clock. Drift beyond 5 minutes invalidates all pre-auth timestamps — exactly this symptom. One w32tm check beats 300 resets.
scenarios.hint: What does every Kerberos exchange depend on besides the password?
evidence: Event 4771: pre-auth failed, clock skew too great — 300 events in 10 min
PDC emulator offset +8 min; last sync 4 days ago

scenarios.title: The Noisy Service Account
scenarios.situation: SIEM: 4,000 Event 4769 in one hour from a single workstation, 40 SPNs, RC4 encryption.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening and what is the immediate containment?
choices: Likely Kerberoasting: harvesting crackable service tickets. Isolate the host, rotate targeted service passwords to 25+ chars (or gMSA), hunt the initial access vector.
Normal backup software behavior — ignore.
Block port 88 at the firewall.
Disable the workstation account and move on.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes the pattern: high-volume TGS requests with weak crypto from one host is textbook Kerberoasting. Containment is host isolation plus killing the crackable material. Blocking 88 breaks all auth.
scenarios.hint: What does legitimate software never do with service tickets?

scenarios.title: The Impossible Admin
scenarios.situation: A non-admin user accessed a server admin share at 3 AM. No 4769 exists on any DC for that access.
scenarios.prompt: What does the missing 4769 suggest, and what is the response?
choices: Silver ticket: forged service ticket needs no KDC contact, so no 4769 is logged. Rotate the service account password twice, find the hash disclosure, review privileged paths.
Logs are broken — fix auditing and wait.
User guessed the local admin password.
Golden ticket — rotate krbtgt now.
scenarios.why: The correct approach reads the negative evidence: access without a KDC-issued ticket means local forgery — a silver ticket. A golden ticket would show anomalous 4768s; the absent 4769 is the silver tell.
scenarios.hint: What event MUST occur for legitimate access — and what does its absence prove?
evidence: SMB session 03:12, no DC 4769 within 1 hour
Service account hash unchanged 4 years; has SPN

scenarios.title: The Helpdesk That Could
scenarios.situation: A junior helpdesk account accessed the finance server as Domain Admin. They claim they only reset passwords.
scenarios.prompt: Which misconfiguration likely enabled this, and how do you confirm?
choices: Unconstrained delegation or RBCD rights: query TrustedForDelegation and msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity, remove unjustified entries, investigate the initial hop separately.
The technician is lying — disable the account.
Password reuse — reset and enable MFA.
Weak SMB signing on finance server.
scenarios.why: The correct approach follows the delegation attack path: low-privilege to DA requires a boundary failure, and delegation misconfiguration is the classic Kerberos-shaped hole. Inventory first, then investigate initial access separately.
scenarios.hint: How does a non-admin gain admin tickets without an admin password?
evidence: PRINT-SRV-02: TrustedForDelegation=TRUE; tech had local admin via GPO
TGS for cifs/finance as administrator from print server

scenarios.title: The Silent Account
scenarios.situation: Threat intel warns of AS-REP roasting against your domain.
scenarios.prompt: What is the precise query and remediation order?
choices: Get-ADUser -Filter {DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true}: every hit is roastable credential-free. Enable pre-auth first (test legacy), then rotate those passwords in case already harvested.
Disable accounts with recent failed logons.
Enable lockout policy.
Find 'password never expires' accounts — same thing.
scenarios.why: The correct approach targets the exact attribute. Lockout does not help (no failed logons in roasting). Order matters: enable pre-auth to stop future harvesting, then rotate to kill already-stolen material.
scenarios.hint: Which single attribute makes AS-REP roasting possible?

scenarios.title: The RC4 Sunset
scenarios.situation: Mandate: disable RC4 Kerberos domain-wide. App team warns something old will break.
scenarios.prompt: How do you execute safely?
choices: Baseline 4768/4769 encryption types for two weeks to find RC4-only clients, remediate or exception them, then disable via GPO in a window with rollback ready.
Disable immediately — mandates are not negotiable.
Leave RC4 on; risk is theoretical.
Disable on DCs only.
scenarios.why: The correct approach is evidence-driven: logs reveal exactly who negotiates RC4. Exceptions get owners and sunset dates. Blind disabling causes an outage you own.
scenarios.hint: What data tells you who breaks before you break them?
evidence: RC4 (0x17): 3 print servers, 1 NAS — all documented

scenarios.title: The Unarmored Exchange
scenarios.situation: You are hardening Kerberos. FAST (armoring) is available but not enforced.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe rollout sequence?
choices: Audit mode first: enable 'Require FAST' in audit to identify clients that break, remediate or exception them, then enforce — armoring without a client inventory causes an outage.
Enforce immediately — armoring is strictly better.
FAST is unnecessary with AES enabled.
Only enforce on DCs.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats every Kerberos hardening like the RC4 sunset: baseline, exception, enforce. Armoring breaks legacy clients silently if you skip the audit.
scenarios.hint: What broke last time you enforced a Kerberos change blind?
evidence: Mixed client fleet; some legacy systems present

domains.name: Group Policy Security

scenarios.title: The Policy That Never Applied
scenarios.situation: You linked a hardening GPO to the Workstations OU, but gpresult shows it not applying to half the machines.
scenarios.prompt: What is the systematic troubleshooting order?
choices: Check link/scope/filter first (gpresult /r: is it denied by filter?), then replication (repadmin), then client processing (gpupdate /force, Event 1500s) — most 'not applying' is scope or filter, not corruption.
Delete and recreate the GPO.
Reboot all affected machines.
Raise the GPO link order to 1.
scenarios.why: The correct approach walks the application chain in order: link exists? filter allows? replicated? client processed? Each step is a 30-second check; recreating the GPO discards the actual (usually trivial) cause.
scenarios.hint: What are the three gates between 'linked' and 'applied'?
evidence: Filtered to 'Workstation-Admins' — machines are not members

scenarios.title: The Midnight GPO Change
scenarios.situation: At 2 AM, a GPO deploying ransomware-laced logon scripts was linked at the domain root. Morning will be catastrophic.
scenarios.prompt: What is the immediate response?
choices: Emergency: disable the GPO link immediately (stops further application), isolate affected machines, restore clean SYSVOL/GPO from backup, force password resets for exposed privileged accounts, then hunt the initial access.
Delete the GPO — fastest removal.
Let it apply and clean machines in the morning.
Restore from backup first, then disable.
scenarios.why: The correct approach stops the bleeding first: disabling the link halts new infections in seconds while you work. Deleting destroys forensic evidence; restoring before disabling lets the malicious version re-replicate.
scenarios.hint: What stops new infections in the next 60 seconds?
evidence: GPO modified 02:14 by compromised helpdesk account
Linked at domain root — all 800 machines targeted

scenarios.title: The Legacy App Break
scenarios.situation: You disabled NTLM via GPO. Monday: the 15-year-old payroll app is down, and payroll runs Wednesday.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong in the change process, and what now?
choices: No application dependency baseline before disabling an auth protocol: immediately create a scoped exception GPO for the payroll servers (documented, time-boxed), run payroll, then plan the app's remediation path.
Re-enable NTLM domain-wide permanently.
Tell payroll to use the new system.
The app team should have spoken up.
scenarios.why: The correct approach owns the change failure (no baseline) while protecting the business (scoped exception, not domain-wide rollback). The exception gets an owner and sunset date — not permanent residence.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between a rollback and a scoped exception?
evidence: Payroll app down; 200 employees affected Wednesday
NTLM disabled domain-wide Friday, no app inventory

scenarios.title: The Kiosk Mystery
scenarios.situation: Kiosk machines apply user policies meant for office staff, exposing admin tools on public terminals.
scenarios.prompt: What GPO feature fixes this, and how?
choices: Loopback processing in Replace mode on the kiosk OU: computer policy replaces the user's normal user-policy set with the kiosk lockdown set, regardless of who logs on.
Block Inheritance on the kiosk OU.
Move kiosks to a separate domain.
Deny logon to office staff on kiosks.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses the purpose-built mechanism: loopback exists exactly for 'this computer's user policy must win.' Block Inheritance would also block needed policies; separate domains are overkill.
scenarios.hint: Whose user policies should apply on a shared special-purpose machine?
evidence: Office staff user policies applying to kiosk sessions

scenarios.title: The Admin Workstation Gap
scenarios.situation: Admins RDP to servers from their daily-use workstations. You must enforce PAW usage via GPO.
scenarios.prompt: What is the enforcement design?
choices: Authentication Silo + GPO: privileged accounts only authenticate from PAW computer accounts; GPO denies interactive logon for Tier 0 creds elsewhere; monitor violations as security events.
Send an email telling admins to use PAWs.
Block RDP entirely.
It cannot be enforced technically.
scenarios.why: The correct approach makes the secure path the only path: Authentication Policies/Silos technically prevent privileged creds from working outside PAWs, and violations become detectable events rather than policy suggestions.
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between asking and enforcing?
evidence: DA creds used from 40 different workstations last month

scenarios.title: The Silent Change
scenarios.situation: A GPO was modified last week. Nobody knows what changed or by whom.
scenarios.prompt: What should have been in place, and what do you do now?
choices: Directory auditing (Event 5136) on GPO objects + AGPM change control + GPO backups: now, diff current GPO against the last backup (Backup-GPO versioning) to identify the change, then implement the missing controls.
Restore the oldest backup available.
Ask around to find who changed it.
It is probably fine — move on.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recovers the fact (backup diff shows exactly what changed) and fixes the process gap (auditing + AGPM + backups) so 'nobody knows' never recurs.
scenarios.hint: How do you determine what changed without auditing?
evidence: No 5136 events — directory auditing not enabled

scenarios.title: The Untested Restore
scenarios.situation: You have GPO backups but have never tested restoring one.
scenarios.prompt: What is the minimal meaningful test?
choices: Import a backed-up GPO to an isolated test OU, verify settings apply via gpresult, then delete the test import — proves the backup is restorable without touching production.
Restore directly to production to be thorough.
Backups are fine — the backup job is green.
Document the backup location.
scenarios.why: The correct approach proves restorability without production risk: the isolated import validates the backup format, the settings, and your procedure in one safe test.
scenarios.hint: What does a green backup job prove about restores?
evidence: Green jobs for 1 year; zero restore tests

domains.name: AD Replication and Recovery

scenarios.title: The Growing Backlog
scenarios.situation: repadmin /queue shows 4,000 pending replications on DC02, growing hourly. Users report stale group memberships.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnostic order?
choices: Check replication health first: repadmin /showrepl for errors, /replsummary for partners, network path to the source DC, disk space, then event logs — backlog is a symptom of a broken partnership, not the disease.
Run repadmin /syncall /force to clear the queue.
Reboot DC02.
Demote and repromote DC02.
scenarios.why: The correct approach diagnoses before forcing: /syncall on a broken partnership just re-fails. The queue tells you volume; /showrepl tells you why (auth failure? network? USN?). Fix the partnership and the queue drains itself.
scenarios.hint: Is the queue the problem or a symptom?
evidence: Error 8524: DSA operation unable to proceed

scenarios.title: The Cross-Country Logon
scenarios.situation: Users in the new Austin office authenticate to the Boston DC over the WAN. Logons take 90 seconds.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: Missing AD Site/subnet mapping: Austin subnets are not defined in AD Sites, so clients get random DC assignment. Create the Austin site, map subnets, verify with nltest /dsgetsite.
The WAN link is too slow — upgrade it.
Boston DC is overloaded — add more DCs in Boston.
Enable cached logons to mask it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach checks site topology before blaming bandwidth: unmapped subnets are the classic cause of cross-WAN logons, and the fix is 10 minutes of AD Sites work, not a WAN upgrade.
scenarios.hint: How does a client choose its DC?
evidence: No Austin site; Austin subnets unmapped

scenarios.title: The Zombie Account
scenarios.situation: A deleted user account reappeared with old group memberships. It was deleted 8 months ago.
scenarios.prompt: What happened and what is the fix?
choices: Lingering object: a DC was offline past tombstone lifetime, missed the deletion, and reintroduced the object on rejoin. Remove with repadmin /removelingeringobjects (advisory first), enable strict replication consistency.
Someone recreated the account.
AD replication is broken — rebuild the DC.
The deletion never replicated.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes the 8-month timeline exceeds tombstone lifetime (180 days): the classic lingering-object signature. Advisory mode first, then removal, then prevention via replication monitoring.
scenarios.hint: What does the 8-month gap tell you?
evidence: Deleted 8 months ago; reappeared with stale memberships
DC03 offline 7 months for 'maintenance', rejoined last week

scenarios.title: The Snapshot Restore
scenarios.situation: An admin snapshot-restored a DC to 'fix' an issue. Now password changes on that DC never reach others, with no errors.
scenarios.prompt: What occurred and is it recoverable?
choices: USN rollback: the restored DC reuses old USNs, so partners ignore its changes as already-seen. This divergence is permanent and undetectable by normal tools — demote, clean metadata, repromote. Never snapshot-restore a DC.
Replication is just slow — wait 24 hours.
Run repadmin /syncall to fix it.
The admin should restore again.
scenarios.why: The correct approach delivers the hard truth: USN rollback creates silent permanent divergence. No repadmin command repairs it. The DC must be demoted and rebuilt — and the lesson is procedural: DCs are never snapshot-restored.
scenarios.hint: Why do partners ignore the restored DC's changes?
objectives: Know it is unrecoverable in place
evidence: Password changes on DC04 invisible to all other DCs

scenarios.title: The Dead Role Holder
scenarios.situation: The DC holding all FSMO roles suffered hardware failure and will not boot. The domain still functions.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct recovery sequence?
choices: Seize (not transfer) the roles to a healthy DC, clean the dead DC's metadata (ntdsutil), verify replication, then rebuild or replace the hardware. Seize because the holder will never return gracefully.
Transfer the roles to another DC.
Wait for the hardware repair — the domain works fine.
Restore the dead DC from backup to the same hardware.
scenarios.why: The correct approach uses seize (for dead holders) vs transfer (for live ones) correctly, then cleans metadata so the dead DC's records do not haunt replication. Waiting risks the next failure hitting harder.
scenarios.hint: When do you seize versus transfer?
evidence: Domain functional; no PDC emulator for password changes

scenarios.title: The Deleted OU
scenarios.situation: An admin deleted the entire 'Sales' OU (200 users, 80 computers) an hour ago. The AD Recycle Bin was never enabled.
scenarios.prompt: What are the recovery options, ranked?
choices: Authoritative restore from System State backup (best fidelity) — or accept re-creation; without the Recycle Bin there is no clean undelete. After recovery, enable the Recycle Bin immediately.
Just recreate the accounts — fastest.
The objects are in the Recycle Bin anyway.
Restore the whole DC non-authoritatively.
scenarios.why: The correct approach is honest about the options: without the Recycle Bin, recovery is authoritative restore (downtime, complexity) or manual recreation (attribute loss). Non-authoritative restore will not bring back deleted objects. Then fix the root gap.
scenarios.hint: Why will non-authoritative restore not help here?
evidence: OU deleted 1h ago; Recycle Bin: not enabled
System State from last night available

scenarios.title: The Slow Decay
scenarios.situation: Replication has been 'fine' but user complaints about stale data are increasing over months.
scenarios.prompt: What monitoring would have caught this early?
choices: Trended repadmin metrics: queue depth, max delta, error counts over time with alerting on degradation — point-in-time checks miss slow decay; trends reveal it months before users complain.
More frequent manual repadmin checks.
Bigger DCs.
It is normal for replication to slow over time.
scenarios.why: The correct approach instruments the decay: slow degradation is invisible to spot checks but obvious in trends. The alert fires when the slope changes, not when users complain.
scenarios.hint: Why do point-in-time checks miss this?
evidence: Stale group memberships increasing over 3 months

domains.name: DNS and DHCP Services

scenarios.title: The Vanishing Domain
scenarios.situation: Clients cannot find the domain: 'no logon servers available.' DCs are up, pingable, and replicating.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely DNS-layer cause?
choices: Missing or stale DC SRV records in DNS: verify _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.lab resolves to live DCs; check secure dynamic updates and scavenging did not eat them.
The DCs need rebooting.
Kerberos is broken.
The clients need rejoining to the domain.
scenarios.why: The correct approach checks the AD-DNS dependency first: 'no logon servers' with healthy DCs screams SRV record failure. Ping proves IP; only SRV proves service location.
scenarios.hint: What must DNS provide for logon beyond name resolution?

scenarios.title: The Strange Redirect
scenarios.situation: Users report the intranet portal 'looks different' and asks for credentials twice. The portal server is untouched.
scenarios.prompt: What DNS attack fits, and what do you check?
choices: DNS spoofing/poisoning redirecting clients to a lookalike: check the actual resolved IPs vs authoritative, inspect DNS logs for anomalies, consider DNSSEC; treat as active credential harvesting until ruled out.
The portal was redesigned — ask the web team.
User browser caches are stale.
It is a phishing email, not DNS.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats unexpected credential prompts plus visual differences as a harvesting indicator until proven otherwise: verify resolution integrity first, assume compromise of the response path.
scenarios.hint: How do you distinguish a redesign from a redirect?

scenarios.title: The Wrong Gateway
scenarios.situation: Half the subnet gets IP addresses with gateway 192.168.99.1 (unknown). Traffic is being intercepted.
scenarios.prompt: What is happening and the immediate fix?
choices: Rogue DHCP server: locate via switch snooping tables / MAC, disconnect it, verify authorized servers only, investigate the device as a potential intentional implant.
Reconfigure the legitimate DHCP scope.
The gateway changed — update documentation.
Reboot the affected clients.
scenarios.why: The correct approach identifies the rogue server as the attack (or misconfiguration) and treats the device as hostile until proven otherwise: traffic interception via DHCP is a classic MITM.
scenarios.hint: What device is answering DHCP faster than yours?

scenarios.title: The Monday Morning Flood
scenarios.situation: Monday 8 AM: 200 new contractors, no one gets an IP. Scope shows 0% available.
scenarios.prompt: Immediate fix and lasting fix?
choices: Immediate: shorten lease duration temporarily and/or add addresses (superscope/expand); lasting: right-size scopes for peak, monitor utilization with alerts at 80%, plan for growth events.
Tell contractors to come back tomorrow.
Reboot the DHCP server.
Switch everyone to static IPs.
scenarios.why: The correct approach separates the fire (get addresses now via shorter leases/expanded scope) from the prevention (utilization monitoring and event-aware capacity planning).
scenarios.hint: What buys addresses in the next 10 minutes vs prevents next quarter?
evidence: 200 contractors started today, unannounced to IT

scenarios.title: The Chatty Workstation
scenarios.situation: DNS logs show one workstation making 50,000 queries/day to random-looking subdomains of an external domain.
scenarios.prompt: What does this indicate?
choices: Likely DNS tunneling/C2: encode data in subdomain labels. Isolate the host, capture full query logs, hunt for the implant, review what data the host touches.
A misconfigured application.
Normal telemetry.
The DNS server is looping.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes the tunneling signature: high-volume, high-entropy subdomains to one external domain is the textbook DNS exfiltration/C2 pattern. Treat as compromise until forensics says otherwise.
scenarios.hint: What legitimate workload looks like this?
evidence: Workstation in finance, user on vacation

scenarios.title: The Silent VLAN
scenarios.situation: New VLAN 40: clients get APIPA addresses (169.254.x.x). DHCP server is healthy, other VLANs fine.
scenarios.prompt: What is missing?
choices: DHCP relay (ip helper-address) on the VLAN 40 gateway: broadcasts do not cross routers, so the new VLAN's requests never reach the DHCP server. Add the helper and verify.
The DHCP server needs a reboot.
VLAN 40 needs its own DHCP server.
Clients need static IPs on new VLANs.
scenarios.why: The correct approach knows broadcasts do not route: every new VLAN needs either a local DHCP server or a relay. APIPA + healthy server + other VLANs fine = relay missing.
scenarios.hint: Why do other VLANs work but not this one?
evidence: VLAN 40 SVI: no ip helper-address configured

scenarios.title: The Signing Decision
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks whether to deploy DNSSEC on the AD zones.
scenarios.prompt: What is the honest assessment?
choices: DNSSEC authenticates DNS data (not encrypts); for AD-integrated internal zones the value is lower than for public zones — recommend piloting on a test zone, measuring operational cost (key management), then deciding with data.
Deploy immediately — DNSSEC is always worth it.
DNSSEC is unnecessary — firewalls handle it.
Only sign the public website zone.
scenarios.why: The correct approach is honest about cost-benefit: DNSSEC has real operational overhead (key ceremonies, rollovers), and its value differs by zone type. Pilot first, decide with data.
scenarios.hint: What does DNSSEC actually provide, and at what cost?
evidence: Should we DNSSEC-sign internal AD zones?

domains.name: PowerShell for AD Defense

scenarios.title: The 20-Minute Query
scenarios.situation: Your 'list all users' script takes 20 minutes and times out on the WAN.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Move filtering to the DC: replace Get-ADUser -Filter * | Where-Object {...} with precise -Filter and -SearchBase so the DC returns only matches — seconds instead of timeouts.
Run it on the DC directly.
Schedule it overnight.
Get a faster workstation.
scenarios.why: The correct approach fixes the data-movement problem: pulling 50k objects to filter locally is the bottleneck, and -Filter/-SearchBase push the work to the DC where the index lives.
scenarios.hint: Where does the filtering happen in each version?

scenarios.title: The 500 Broken Accounts
scenarios.situation: A bulk import created 500 users with wrong UPN suffixes. They are already being used.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong and what is the recovery?
choices: No WhatIf/pilot: the CSV mapping error hit all 500 at once. Recovery: script the UPN correction (Set-ADUser -UserPrincipalName) since accounts are live; then mandate WhatIf + 5-account pilot for all bulk ops.
Delete all 500 and re-import.
Manually fix each in ADUC.
Blame the CSV provider.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recovers without destroying live accounts (scripted correction) and fixes the process (WhatIf + pilot gates). Deleting live accounts breaks in-flight work.
scenarios.hint: What gate would have caught this at 5 accounts instead of 500?

scenarios.title: The Quiet Escalation
scenarios.situation: An attacker gained Domain Admin without any password attack. Logs show only legitimate helpdesk actions.
scenarios.prompt: Which AD misconfiguration enables this, and how do you find it?
choices: Dangerous ACLs (GenericAll/WriteDacl) on privileged objects: query AD ACLs for non-admin principals with write rights over admin targets (e.g., helpdesk group with GenericAll on Domain Admins) — the attacker modified, then used, the rights.
The logs are incomplete.
Zero-day in Windows.
The helpdesk account was already DA.
scenarios.why: The correct approach looks at authorization, not authentication: ACL-based escalation leaves only 'legitimate' actions in the log because the actions WERE authorized — wrongly. ACL auditing finds the misconfiguration.
scenarios.hint: What is logged when an authorized-but-wrong permission is used?
evidence: All actions by helpdesk account were 'permitted'

scenarios.title: The Standing Admin
scenarios.situation: Helpdesk staff hold Domain Admin 'because they need to reset passwords.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the least-privilege redesign?
choices: JEA endpoint: helpdesk gets Reset-ADAccountPassword/Unlock-ADAccount scoped to non-privileged OUs via a constrained endpoint — full job capability, zero standing DA, every action transcribed.
Remove their admin rights and let managers reset passwords.
Keep DA but require MFA.
It is fine — they are trusted.
scenarios.why: The correct approach removes the standing privilege while preserving capability: JEA gives exactly the needed cmdlets on exactly the needed scope. Trust is not a control.
scenarios.hint: What is the minimum capability the job actually requires?

scenarios.title: The Ghost Admins
scenarios.situation: Audit finds 30 enabled accounts with AdminCount=1 that have not logged on in over a year.
scenarios.prompt: What is the risk and the remediation?
choices: Dormant privileged accounts are ideal persistence: no one notices their use. Disable immediately, investigate any recent auth, then implement quarterly stale-privileged review with automatic disable policy.
They are harmless if unused.
Delete them all right now.
Force password changes.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats dormancy + privilege as the highest-risk combination: attackers love accounts nobody watches. Disable first (reversible), investigate, then automate the review so it never recurs.
scenarios.hint: Why is an unused admin account more dangerous than an active one?

scenarios.title: The Score That Stings
scenarios.situation: PingCastle scores your domain 85/100 risk (high). Management asks what to fix first.
scenarios.prompt: How do you prioritize?
choices: Risk-ordered, effort-weighted: start with high-risk + low-effort (stale admins, pre-auth, anonymous access), then high-risk structural (delegation, krbtgt age) with planned windows — present as a phased roadmap, not a panic list.
Fix everything immediately.
Dispute the score — the tool is too strict.
Hire a consultant to interpret it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach converts a scary score into an executable plan: quick wins build momentum and credibility while structural fixes get proper windows. The score is a prioritization tool, not a verdict.
scenarios.hint: What builds momentum while reducing the most risk?
objectives: Use scores as tools not verdicts
evidence: Score 85/100; top findings: stale admins, RC4, unconstrained delegation

scenarios.title: The Monthly Ask
scenarios.situation: Leadership wants a monthly AD security posture report.
scenarios.prompt: What makes the report effective?
choices: Trended metrics with owners: stale privileged count (down 40→12), LAPS coverage (→100%), delegation findings — each metric has a trend, an owner, and a next action. Snapshots inform; trends persuade.
A dump of all AD users and groups.
The PingCastle score alone.
A narrative essay about security.
scenarios.why: The correct approach gives leadership decisions, not data: trends show progress, owners show accountability, next actions show the plan. Raw dumps delegate the analysis to the busiest people.
scenarios.hint: What does leadership need to decide from this report?

domains.name: AD Backup and Disaster Recovery

scenarios.title: The Untested Backup
scenarios.situation: Audit asks: 'When did you last test an AD restore?' The answer is never.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response and action?
choices: Honest answer plus immediate plan: schedule an isolated-lab restore test this quarter, document the procedure gaps found, and make restore testing a recurring control — an untested backup is not a backup.
Claim the backups are fine — the agent shows green.
Test in production to be thorough.
It is fine; restores rarely needed.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats the audit finding as legitimate: green agent lights verify backup jobs, not restorability. The isolated test finds the DSRM password gaps, media issues, and procedure errors before they matter.
scenarios.hint: What does a green backup job actually prove?
evidence: 'Show me the last successful AD restore test.'
All jobs green for 2 years; zero restore tests

scenarios.title: The Wrong Restore Type
scenarios.situation: A DC failed. The admin performed an authoritative restore of the entire database 'to be safe.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the risk of this choice?
choices: Authoritative full restore can resurrect long-deleted objects and roll back legitimate changes domain-wide — for a simple DC failure, non-authoritative (rebuild + replicate) was correct. Now verify for zombie objects.
No risk — authoritative is always safer.
The DC will not boot.
Replication will be faster.
scenarios.why: The correct approach matches restore type to scenario: authoritative is for 'bad data replicated everywhere,' not 'one DC died.' The over-broad choice creates the exact data-integrity problem it aimed to avoid.
scenarios.hint: What does authoritative restore do to legitimately deleted objects?
evidence: Full authoritative restore for single DC hardware failure

scenarios.title: The Encrypted Backups
scenarios.situation: Ransomware encrypted production AND the online backup repository. Only offline tapes from 30 days ago survive.
scenarios.prompt: What does this teach about backup architecture?
choices: 3-2-1 with offline/air-gapped copies: ransomware targets backups first. Recovery now means 30-day-old AD (tombstone risk, massive divergence) — rebuild strategy, not simple restore. Future: immutable offline copies tested regularly.
Pay the ransom to get the backups back.
30-day-old AD is fine — just restore it.
Backups are useless against ransomware.
scenarios.why: The correct approach faces the brutal facts: 30-day-old AD exceeds safe restore windows and the divergence is enormous. The lesson is architectural — offline/immutable copies — learned at maximum cost.
scenarios.hint: Why is a 30-day-old AD backup dangerous to restore?
evidence: Production + online backups encrypted; tapes 30 days old
180 days — restore possible but divergence massive

scenarios.title: The Unknown Password
scenarios.situation: During a DC recovery, nobody knows the DSRM password. It was set years ago by a departed admin.
scenarios.prompt: How do you prevent and recover from this?
choices: Recover: ntdsutil 'set dsrm password' on a running DC (or reset via command line) — then vault it in the break-glass store with the forest recovery runbook. Prevention: DSRM password in the offline vault, rotated with admin turnover.
Reinstall the DC — DSRM is unrecoverable.
Skip DSRM mode in the recovery.
Guess common passwords.
scenarios.why: The correct approach knows DSRM passwords are resettable from a running DC, then fixes the process: break-glass vault + turnover rotation. The password is infrastructure, not trivia.
scenarios.hint: Where should the DSRM password live?
evidence: DSRM password unknown; last admin departed 2 years ago

scenarios.title: The Seize Decision
scenarios.situation: PDC emulator is down for hardware repair, ETA 4 hours. Password changes are failing.
scenarios.prompt: Seize the role now or wait?
choices: Wait with a deadline: 4-hour ETA is within tolerance for most environments; seizing is for dead-or-extended outages. Set a decision point (e.g., 6 hours or repair failure) and prepare the seize procedure in parallel.
Seize immediately — password changes are critical.
Never seize; always wait for repair.
Transfer the role to the broken DC later.
scenarios.why: The correct approach weighs the cost of seizing (cannot gracefully return the role; the old holder must never rejoin uncleaned) against the outage cost. A 4-hour repair favors waiting with a prepared fallback.
scenarios.hint: What is the irreversible cost of seizing?
evidence: PDC emulator down; repair ETA 4h; password changes failing

scenarios.title: The Ghost DC
scenarios.situation: A DC was decommissioned by simply powering it off 6 months ago. Replication errors reference it constantly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the cleanup?
choices: Metadata cleanup via ntdsutil (or ADUC/ADSI for modern versions): remove the NTDS settings, server, and computer objects; verify DNS SRV cleanup; confirm repadmin is clean. Then document the proper demotion procedure.
Just power it back on and demote properly.
Ignore the errors — the DC is gone.
Reinstall a new DC with the same name.
scenarios.why: The correct approach removes the dead metadata authoritatively: powering it back on after 6 months risks USN/lingering issues, and ignoring it poisons replication and service location indefinitely.
scenarios.hint: What still references the dead DC?
evidence: Stale SRV records for the dead DC

scenarios.title: The Silent Failure
scenarios.situation: Backups have been failing for 3 weeks. Nobody noticed until the audit.
scenarios.prompt: What monitoring was missing?
choices: Backup success alerting with paging (not email): failed backup = page, backup age > 24h = page — plus a weekly human review of the backup dashboard. Silent failures are a monitoring design failure.
Better backup software.
More frequent backups.
The audit should not have access.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats backup monitoring as production monitoring: failures page, age is tracked, humans review weekly. Three silent weeks means the alerting was designed to be ignored.
scenarios.hint: How long can backups fail before someone must know?
evidence: 3 weeks of failed jobs; discovered by external audit

domains.name: Hybrid Identity Security

scenarios.title: The Stopped Sync
scenarios.situation: New users created on-prem are not appearing in Entra ID. Last successful sync was 3 days ago.
scenarios.prompt: Diagnostic order?
choices: Check the sync scheduler and service health (Get-ADSyncScheduler, MIISClient), then export errors, then connector credentials/password expiry, then network to Entra — most sync stops are scheduler, credential, or export-error issues.
Reinstall Entra Connect.
Manually create the users in the cloud.
It will catch up on its own.
scenarios.why: The correct approach works the sync pipeline in order: scheduler → connectors → export errors. Reinstalling destroys forensic state; manual creation causes future sync collisions.
scenarios.hint: What are the stages of a sync cycle?

scenarios.title: The Prompt That Should Not Appear
scenarios.situation: Domain-joined users are suddenly prompted for passwords on cloud apps; Seamless SSO worked last week.
scenarios.prompt: What broke?
choices: Seamless SSO Kerberos chain: verify the AZUREADSSOACC computer account (password/kerberos key), the intranet zone configuration, and that the feature is still enabled in Entra Connect — SSO is Kerberos, so treat it like Kerberos troubleshooting.
Users forgot their passwords.
Entra ID is down.
Reinstall the Connect client.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes Seamless SSO as Kerberos with extra steps: the failure modes are Kerberos failure modes (key mismatch, zone config, SPN issues).
scenarios.hint: What must be true for silent Kerberos SSO to work?
evidence: Group Policy updated Friday — Internet zone settings

scenarios.title: The Quiet Replication
scenarios.situation: EDR flags Event 4662 with directory replication GUIDs from a non-DC host.
scenarios.prompt: What does this indicate and what is the response?
choices: DCSync attack: credential theft via replication protocol. Isolate the host, force-rotate krbtgt TWICE, rotate all privileged credentials, hunt for persistence — DCSync means total domain compromise until proven otherwise.
Normal replication traffic.
A misconfigured backup agent.
Ignore — EDR false positives are common.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats DCSync as the worst-case indicator: it yields every hash in the domain. The response is full credential rotation, not single-host cleanup.
scenarios.hint: What can an attacker do with DCSync rights?
evidence: Replication GUIDs accessed from non-DC host 10.0.7.44

scenarios.title: The Blocked Break-Glass
scenarios.situation: A Conditional Access misconfiguration locked out all admins, including the break-glass accounts.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong and what is the recovery?
choices: Break-glass accounts were not excluded from CA policies: recover via the documented emergency procedure (they should be cloud-only, MFA-registered, monitored, and excluded from ALL CA). Then fix the policy and add the exclusion guardrail.
Disable Conditional Access entirely.
Wait for Microsoft support.
The break-glass passwords must be wrong.
scenarios.why: The correct approach planned for this: break-glass accounts exist precisely for CA lockouts, so they must be excluded from every policy. Recovery uses them; prevention is the exclusion plus alerting on their use.
scenarios.hint: What is the purpose of a break-glass account?
evidence: 'Block all legacy auth' applied to 'All users' including break-glass
Zero admin access to Entra portal

scenarios.title: The Cloud-to-OnPrem Write
scenarios.situation: Password writeback is enabled. An attacker compromises a cloud helpdesk admin account.
scenarios.prompt: What is the blast radius?
choices: On-prem AD: writeback lets the cloud account reset on-prem passwords — the cloud compromise becomes a domain compromise path. Scope writeback tightly, monitor cloud admin roles as Tier 0 equivalent.
Only cloud accounts are at risk.
Writeback is read-only.
MFA in the cloud prevents this.
scenarios.why: The correct approach maps the trust direction: writeback is a deliberate on-prem write path from the cloud. Cloud admin roles must be treated with on-prem Tier 0 seriousness.
scenarios.hint: Which direction does writeback flow?
evidence: Password writeback: enabled for all users
Cloud helpdesk admin — can reset any synced user's on-prem password

scenarios.title: The Auth Method Decision
scenarios.situation: Leadership asks: PHS, PTA, or federation for the new hybrid deployment?
scenarios.prompt: What is the defensible recommendation?
choices: PHS as default: simplest, survives on-prem outages, Microsoft-recommended. PTA only if policy forbids hash sync; federation only for documented requirements PHS/PTA cannot meet (complex SSO claims). Document the decision.
Federation — maximum control.
PTA — no hashes in the cloud ever.
All three for redundancy.
scenarios.why: The correct approach defaults to simplicity and resilience: PHS meets most requirements with the least infrastructure. Complexity must be justified by requirements, not preferences.
scenarios.hint: What requirement would force you off PHS?
evidence: Standard workforce; no exotic claims needs; uptime priority

scenarios.title: The Untested Break-Glass
scenarios.situation: The cloud break-glass account has never been tested. A CA misconfiguration just locked out all admins.
scenarios.prompt: What happens now?
choices: Attempt break-glass logon per the runbook; if it works, fix CA; if not, escalate to Microsoft support with tenant recovery — then institutionalize quarterly testing so this never recurs. This is why untested break-glass is Schrodinger's access.
Wait for the CA policy to expire.
The break-glass will work — it was set up correctly.
Disable Conditional Access via PowerShell (no admin access needed).
scenarios.why: The correct approach follows the runbook while being honest about the gamble: untested credentials may fail. The real fix is the process change afterward.
scenarios.hint: What was the quarterly test supposed to prevent?
evidence: All admins locked out; break-glass never tested

scenarios.title: The Slow Spray
scenarios.situation: 4625 failures: 3 per hour per account, across 500 accounts, from rotating source IPs. No lockouts triggered.
scenarios.prompt: What is this and what is the response?
choices: Password spraying below lockout thresholds: block the source ASNs at the edge, force MFA enrollment, hunt for any successful 4624 from those sources (the spray may have worked somewhere), review for compromised accounts.
Normal failed logons — users forget passwords.
Increase the lockout threshold.
The SIEM is misconfigured.
scenarios.why: The correct approach recognizes the low-and-slow pattern designed to evade lockouts: the response is edge blocking plus hunting for successes, because the spray's goal was one valid login among the noise.
scenarios.hint: Why 3 per hour per account?
evidence: 2 successful logons from spray source IPs — investigate

scenarios.title: The New Admin
scenarios.situation: Event 4728: a user was added to Domain Admins at 2 AM by a service account.
scenarios.prompt: What is the investigation order?
choices: Treat as compromise until proven otherwise: isolate the added account (disable), investigate the service account's compromise (it should never do this), review what the new DA did, rotate credentials — legitimate DA grants do not happen at 2 AM via service accounts.
Ask the service account owner if it was planned.
Remove the user from DA and close the ticket.
It is probably a scheduled task.
scenarios.why: The correct approach assumes breach for impossible-hour privilege grants via wrong actors: the investigation order is contain (disable), then determine legitimacy — not the reverse.
scenarios.hint: What is wrong with the actor, not just the action?
evidence: 02:14: user added to Domain Admins by svc-backup
svc-backup never modifies groups; changes require CAB approval

scenarios.title: The Empty Log
scenarios.situation: The DC's Security log was cleared (Event 1102) at 3 AM. No authorized maintenance was scheduled.
scenarios.prompt: What does this mean and what now?
choices: Log clearing is attacker tradecraft: assume active compromise — isolate the DC, preserve what forensic artifacts remain (memory, forwarded copies), hunt across the fleet for lateral movement, full incident response.
The log just rolled over.
Re-enable logging and move on.
Check who cleared it and ask why.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats 1102 at 3 AM with no change record as a compromise indicator, not an admin action: the priority is preserving remaining evidence (forwarded logs, memory) before the attacker finishes.
scenarios.hint: Why do attackers clear logs, and what does that tell you about timing?
evidence: Security log cleared 03:07, no change record
Forwarded events stop at 03:06 — gap after

scenarios.title: The Noisy Rule
scenarios.situation: A new detection fires 200 times a day, all false positives. Analysts now ignore it.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Tune with data: analyze the false positives for a distinguishing feature, adjust logic/threshold, document the tuning, re-baseline — and treat 'ignored rule' as an emergency, since real alerts now hide in its noise.
Delete the rule.
Tell analysts to pay attention.
Lower the threshold to catch more.
scenarios.why: The correct approach repairs the signal: an ignored rule is worse than no rule because it creates false confidence. Tuning is driven by false-positive analysis, not guesses.
scenarios.hint: What is worse than no detection?

scenarios.title: The Recon Pattern
scenarios.situation: 4662 events show bulk object reads from a helpdesk workstation — thousands of user/computer objects enumerated.
scenarios.prompt: What does this suggest?
choices: AD reconnaissance (BloodHound-style): someone is mapping attack paths. Isolate, determine if the helpdesk user ran it or their session was hijacked, hunt for follow-on exploitation.
Normal helpdesk activity.
The monitoring is too sensitive.
Inventory software doing its job.
scenarios.why: The correct approach distinguishes legitimate enumeration (targeted, business-hours, known tools) from recon (bulk, unusual host, attack-tool patterns): bulk reads from a helpdesk box is the latter until proven otherwise.
scenarios.hint: What does legitimate helpdesk enumeration look like vs this?
evidence: 12,000 object reads in 20 min from helpdesk WS
Helpdesk tech on vacation this week

scenarios.title: The Missing Events
scenarios.situation: During incident review, you discover the DCs never forwarded logs centrally — each DC only has local logs, and one DC's log was cleared.
scenarios.prompt: What is the architectural fix?
choices: Windows Event Forwarding (or SIEM agents) to a hardened, tamper-evident collector with restricted access — local-only logging is not a logging strategy, it is evidence waiting to be destroyed.
Increase local log sizes.
Back up event logs nightly.
It is fine — most incidents do not need central logs.
scenarios.why: The correct approach centralizes before the incident: forwarded, access-restricted logs survive local clearing. Bigger local logs just take longer to clear.
scenarios.hint: What happens to local logs during a competent attack?
evidence: Local-only logs; one DC's log cleared during incident
Timeline has a 4-hour gap at the critical moment

scenarios.title: The Gap in the Timeline
scenarios.situation: Incident timeline has a 4-hour gap: the collector was down and nobody noticed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix?
choices: Monitor the monitoring: heartbeat alerts from forwarders, collector health checks, gap detection (alert when event flow stops) — the pipeline needs its own SLA and paging.
Bigger collector disk.
It is fine — 4 hours is acceptable.
Collect less data to reduce load.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats the pipeline as critical infrastructure: heartbeat monitoring and flow-gap alerts detect collector failures in minutes. The gap is where the attacker operated unseen.
scenarios.hint: Who watches the watchers?
evidence: 4h missing; collector disk full, no alert
