scenarios.title: The Flat Network
scenarios.situation: Audit finds Domain Admins routinely RDP from their daily workstations to servers and DCs. No PAWs exist.
scenarios.prompt: What is the phased remediation?
choices: Phase 1: deploy PAWs for Tier 0 work + Authentication Silos blocking Tier 0 creds off-PAW; Phase 2: tiered accounts (T0/T1/T2); Phase 3: technical enforcement + monitoring. Each phase reduces lateral blast radius measurably.
Send a policy email forbidding it.
It is fine — the admins are trustworthy.
Block RDP everywhere immediately.
scenarios.why: The correct approach phases technical enforcement: PAWs + silos first (biggest win), then account tiering, then monitoring. Email policies do not stop pass-the-hash; immediate total RDP blocks break operations.
scenarios.hint: What is the highest-leverage first technical control?
evidence: DA creds used from 40 workstations; 0 PAWs

scenarios.title: The Shared Password
scenarios.situation: Every workstation uses the same local admin password, known to all of IT including former employees.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fix and the urgency?
choices: Deploy Windows LAPS immediately (unique per-machine, auto-rotated): the shared password is a domain-wide lateral movement skeleton key. Rotate the shared password TODAY as a stopgap, then LAPS rollout.
Change the shared password quarterly.
It is fine — local admin is not domain admin.
Remove local admin rights from IT.
scenarios.why: The correct approach treats shared local creds as the emergency they are: one compromised workstation yields the key to every workstation. LAPS is the structural fix; immediate rotation is the tourniquet.
scenarios.hint: What does one compromised workstation yield with a shared local password?
evidence: 1 local admin password, 800 workstations, known to 25+ people incl. alumni

scenarios.title: The Eternal Admin
scenarios.situation: Contractors granted 'temporary' Domain Admin 6 months ago still hold it. No one remembers the engagement.
scenarios.prompt: What systemic fix prevents recurrence?
choices: Time-bound JIT elevation with automatic expiry + quarterly access reviews: temporary access must be technically temporary (MemberTimeToLive), not procedurally temporary (a calendar reminder nobody sets).
Remove them now and apologize.
It is fine — they might be needed again.
Ask the contractors if they still need it.
scenarios.why: The correct approach makes temporariness technical: auto-expiring membership cannot be forgotten. Reviews catch what JIT misses. 'Might need again' is how 6-month temporaries happen.
scenarios.hint: Why did 'temporary' become permanent?
evidence: 4 contractor accounts in Domain Admins, added 6 months ago as '2-week engagement'

scenarios.title: The Dumped Credentials
scenarios.situation: EDR alerts: LSASS memory access on a workstation where a Domain Admin logged on yesterday.
scenarios.prompt: What is the immediate response?
choices: Assume the DA credential is compromised: force-rotate krbtgt (twice), reset the DA password, hunt for lateral movement from that workstation, and implement Credential Guard + tiering so DA creds never land on workstations again.
The EDR blocked it — no action needed.
Reboot the workstation.
Change the DA password next week.
scenarios.why: The correct approach assumes the worst from LSASS access after DA logon: the credential is burned until proven otherwise. 'Blocked' is EDR's claim; rotation is cheap insurance against total domain compromise.
scenarios.hint: What is the blast radius of a stolen DA credential?
evidence: LSASS access blocked? PARTIAL — read occurred before block
DA interactive logon on this workstation yesterday

scenarios.title: The Sealed Envelope
scenarios.situation: The break-glass DA account password is in a sealed envelope in the safe. It has not been tested in 2 years.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this picture?
choices: Untested break-glass is Schrodinger's access: test quarterly (verify logon works, then rotate), monitor for ANY use as a critical alert, keep two accounts in case one is compromised. An envelope is storage, not assurance.
Nothing — sealed envelopes are best practice.
Move it to a password manager.
Break-glass accounts are outdated.
scenarios.why: The correct approach tests what must work in emergencies: an untested credential plus an untested procedure equals no recovery capability. Monitoring its use turns it into a tripwire.
scenarios.hint: When will you discover the envelope's password is expired?
evidence: Envelope sealed 2 years; password age unknown; never tested

scenarios.title: The Legacy Setting
scenarios.situation: WDigest is enabled domain-wide 'because an old app needed it in 2019.' No one knows which app.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct action?
choices: Hunt the dependency: enable WDigest auditing/logging to identify actual users, test the suspect app without it, then disable domain-wide — undocumented legacy exceptions are attacker conveniences.
Leave it — the app might still need it.
Disable immediately without investigation.
It is not a real risk.
scenarios.why: The correct approach resolves the uncertainty with data instead of fear: identify the actual consumer, then remove the plaintext-equivalent credential storage. 'Might need it' is not a security control.
scenarios.hint: How do you find what actually uses WDigest?
evidence: No documented app requirement; set in 2019

scenarios.title: The Rubber Stamp
scenarios.situation: Quarterly access reviews are completed in 10 minutes with all access approved, no changes.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong and how do you fix it?
choices: The review is theater: fix with data-driven reviews (show last-use dates, peer comparisons, risk scores), require justification for continued access, and sample-audit the reviewers. Ten-minute blanket approvals are attestation fraud.
The reviewers are efficient.
Quarterly is too frequent — go annual.
Access reviews are unnecessary with JIT.
scenarios.why: The correct approach makes reviews meaningful: present the data that enables judgment (unused access glows), require written justification, and audit the process itself.
scenarios.hint: What information would make blanket approval embarrassing?
evidence: 200 entitlements reviewed in 10 min; 0 revoked in 4 quarters

lessons.title: Active Directory & Identity Defense — Core concepts
concepts: AD structure: domains group into trees, trees into forests; trusts are authentication paths between them — two-way trusts mean compromise can flow either direction.
FSMO roles (Schema Master, Domain Naming Master, PDC Emulator, RID Master, Infrastructure Master) serialize operations that cannot safely run multi-master; know which role gates which task.
Group Policy is the control plane: whoever can edit GPOs can push configuration — and malware — to every machine in scope.
Kerberoasting: any user can request crackable TGS tickets for SPN accounts — defend with long random service passwords and managed service accounts.
AS-REP roasting: accounts with pre-authentication disabled hand crackable responses to anonymous requesters — re-enable pre-auth (the default).
Pass-the-hash/ticket reuses stolen credential material without knowing the password; DCSync/DCShadow abuse replication rights to pull hashes — audit who holds 'Replicating Directory Changes All'.

Hardening: the tiered admin model keeps Tier 0 credentials off lower-tier systems; LAPS gives every machine a unique local admin password; Credential Guard isolates secrets; phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2) stops credential replay.

example.code:
# Hunt for the classic misconfigurations: SPN accounts with old passwords,
# and any account with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled.
# (Run from a domain-joined host with the RSAT AD PowerShell module.)
Import-Module ActiveDirectory
# 1. Accounts with pre-auth disabled (AS-REP roastable):
Get-ADUser -Filter { DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true } -Properties PasswordLastSet |
    Select-Object Name, Enabled, PasswordLastSet
# 2. User accounts with SPNs set (Kerberoastable candidates):
Get-ADUser -Filter { ServicePrincipalName -ne '$null' } -Properties PasswordLastSet |
    Select-Object Name, PasswordLastSet
example.walkthrough: Defense starts with inventory: you cannot protect what you have not enumerated. The first query surfaces accounts with pre-authentication disabled — each one is an anonymous offline-cracking opportunity. The second lists accounts holding SPNs — the Kerberoasting surface. Both are one-line checks that belong in every AD security review, run before any hardening project begins.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating a trust as a network tunnel — it is an authentication relationship, and two-way means risk flows both ways.
Common trap: assuming only Domain Admins can DCSync — any account with replication rights can; audit the permission, not just the group.
Common trap: thinking Kerberos attacks need privileges — Kerberoasting needs only a valid domain user; AS-REP roasting needs no credentials at all.
Common trap: hardening servers while leaving 40 standing Domain Admins on workstations — tiering and LAPS address the credential-exposure path that attackers actually use.

lessons.title: AdFind & AD Reconnaissance Hunting — Core concepts
concepts: AdFind is a free command-line Active Directory query tool (joeware) — a legitimate admin utility that ransomware affiliates adopted as a recon staple. It is dual-use, not malware, and notably absent from LOLBAS: defenders must detect its abuse, not its existence.

The classic recon query set: (objectcategory=person) and (objectcategory=computer) for accounts and hosts, -sc trustdmp / domainlist / dcmodes / adinfo for trust and domain topology, computers_pwdnotreqd for weak-password footholds, and ‘Domain Admins’ for the crown jewels. Each query answers one attacker question.

Detection is behavioral: process creation for adfind.exe (or its renamed twin) plus distinctive command-line tokens, output redirection (>), and a burst threshold — e.g., 3+ distinct query types in two minutes — on hosts and accounts where it is unexpected. Public coverage exists: Sigma (win_susp_adfind, win_ad_find_discovery), Elastic, Splunk, Sentinel, and Microsoft’s Defender hunting query.

Map precisely to ATT&CK discovery: T1087.002 Domain Account, T1069.002 Domain Groups, T1018 Remote System Discovery, T1482 Domain Trust Discovery, T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery. Precise mapping exposes coverage gaps.

Recon outputs are forensic gold: .txt files staged in Temp or staging folders carry creation timestamps that often predate every alert — the earliest hard evidence of when recon began. Extending the timeline can change log-review scope and breach-notification deadlines.
Triage on context: account privilege, host role, parent process (batch/cmd wrappers), time of day, and output destination separate the domain admin’s audit from the affiliate’s recon batch.

example.code: adfind -f (objectcategory=computer) -sc computers_pwdnotreqd > C:\Windows\Temp\c.txt
example.walkthrough: One line, three tells: an objectcategory discovery filter, a canned query for accounts that don’t require passwords, and output redirected to Temp. A domain admin auditing stale machines runs this from a jump host with a ticket; a ransomware affiliate runs it from a workstation at 2 AM inside a batch file. Same syntax — the context is the detection.

pitfalls: Common trap: blocking the filename or hash. Attackers rename adfind.exe freely — match on command-line behavior, not the binary name.
Common trap: alerting on every AdFind execution. Domain admins use it legitimately; without user/host scoping and a burst threshold, the rule is pure noise.
Common trap: ignoring the output files. Deleting Temp ‘junk’ during cleanup can destroy the earliest timeline anchor you have.
Common trap: treating recon as the incident. Discovery is the precursor — the response must hunt what comes next: lateral movement.

lessons.title: assessment Strategy: How to Win
concepts: The assessment rewards applied understanding over memorization — every domain here maps to something you will actually be asked to do
Time management wins: in timed assessments, bank the easy wins first, flag the hard ones, and never leave a question blank
Wrong answers are data: each missed scenario reveals a specific gap. Log it, revisit the lesson, and re-attempt until the pattern clicks
Sleep and spacing beat cramming: 90-minute focused sessions with breaks outperform marathon sessions, especially the week before assessment day

example.code:
The 3-pass method for timed assessments:
  Pass 1 (40% of time): answer everything you know cold
  Pass 2 (40% of time): work the flagged mediums with evidence
  Pass 3 (20% of time): educated guesses on the rest

Never spend 10 minutes on one question while five easy ones wait.
example.walkthrough: Elimination is a skill: practice ruling out two wrong choices fast, then deciding between the final two. Most scenario questions are designed so two options are clearly wrong to a prepared candidate.

pitfalls: Changing answers without new evidence — your first instinct after study is usually right
Perfectionism on one hard question while easy points expire
Studying new material the night before instead of reviewing what you know

concepts: This bootcamp has 15+ domains covering the full Active Directory Defense landscape — from foundations to the capstone project
Core domains teach the must-know systems; the Systems Anatomy domain teaches you to see them as living, connected flows
The capstone project proves you can build and operate a real system end-to-end — this is your interview story
The mock assessment simulates the real assessment so there are no surprises on the day

example.code:
Active Directory Defense mastery map:
  Foundations -> Core systems (domains 2-10)
  -> Systems Anatomy (see it all connected)
  -> Capstone (build it yourself)
  -> Mock (prove it under pressure)
example.walkthrough: Start with: Kerberos Authentication Security. It unlocks everything downstream — the path is sequential for a reason.

pitfalls: Treating all domains as equal — weight your time toward the heaviest-tested areas
Skipping Systems Anatomy — it is the differentiator between passing and excelling
Saving the capstone for 'later' — start it early, iterate as you learn
lessons.try_it: Skim the domain list in the Learn path and note which three domains matter most for your goal. Start there after Start Here.

lessons.title: Kerberos Authentication Deep Dive
concepts: Kerberos is ticket-based: the client authenticates once to the KDC and receives tickets proving identity to services without resending credentials
Three exchanges: AS-REQ/AS-REP (get TGT), TGS-REQ/TGS-REP (get service ticket), AP-REQ/AP-REP (present ticket to service)
Tickets are time-bound (10h TGT default, 5-min clock skew tolerance) — time sync via the PDC emulator is a hard dependency
Pre-authentication (timestamp encrypted with the user key) defeats offline AS-REP roasting when enforced

example.code:
klist tickets
klist purge
# Event IDs: 4768 TGT requested, 4769 service ticket requested,
# 4771 pre-auth failed, 4624/4625 logon success/failure
example.walkthrough: klist shows the living ticket cache. Purge and re-authenticate while watching Event 4768 fire on the DC — that is Act 1 in real time.

pitfalls: Confusing the TGT (identity proof to KDC) with the service ticket (authorization proof to resource)
Forgetting UDP/TCP 88 must be open client-to-DC; clock skew over 5 min breaks everything
Treating Kerberos as magic instead of three concrete, loggable exchanges
lessons.try_it: Run klist on a domain machine. Identify TGT vs service tickets and lifetimes.

lessons.title: Kerberoasting and AS-REP Roasting Defense
concepts: Kerberoasting: any authenticated user can request service tickets for SPN-linked accounts; the encrypted portion can be cracked offline
AS-REP roasting: accounts with pre-auth disabled allow attackers to request crackable AS-REP data with zero credentials
Defenses: 25+ char managed passwords on service accounts, Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) with auto-rotation, disable RC4, enforce pre-auth everywhere
Detection: Event 4769 with RC4 (0x17), unusual TGS volume, honey SPN accounts that should never be requested

example.code:
Get-ADUser -Filter {ServicePrincipalName -ne '$null'} -Properties ServicePrincipalName,PasswordLastSet |
 Select Name,PasswordLastSet
Get-ADUser -Filter {DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true} | Select Name
example.walkthrough: Enumerate SPNs the way an attacker would — then defend each finding: gMSA, 25+ char rotation, or SPN removal.

pitfalls: Same service account password for years — rotation is the defense
RC4 left on 'for compatibility' with no documented owner
No alerting on 4769 volume spikes
lessons.try_it: Audit your lab for pre-auth-disabled accounts and user-account SPNs. Remediate one.

lessons.title: Golden and Silver Ticket Defense
concepts: Golden ticket: forged TGT signed with krbtgt hash — grants anything; requires krbtgt compromise to create
Silver ticket: forged service ticket signed with a service account hash — scoped to one service, needs no DC contact, evades KDC logging
Defense: protect krbtgt; rotate it TWICE (with replication between) after suspected compromise; monitor TGT lifetime anomalies
Detection: 4768 lifetime anomalies; access with no corresponding 4769 (silver ticket tell)

example.code:
# krbtgt rotation (do TWICE):
# 1. Reset krbtgt password
# 2. repadmin /syncall (wait for replication)
# 3. Reset again
# Verify: repadmin /showobjmeta * CN=krbtgt,CN=Users,DC=corp,DC=lab
example.walkthrough: Golden tickets survive password changes of the compromised account — only krbtgt rotation kills them. Practice double-rotation until it is muscle memory.

pitfalls: Rotating krbtgt once — old tickets stay valid until the second rotation
Rotating in business hours — expect an auth storm; use a window
No baseline of normal 4768/4769 volume
lessons.try_it: Document the krbtgt double-rotation runbook with replication wait times.

lessons.title: Delegation: The Hidden Attack Path
concepts: Unconstrained delegation: a compromised server can impersonate ANY user to ANY service — the most dangerous common misconfiguration
Constrained delegation limits target services; resource-based constrained delegation (RBCD) puts control with the resource owner
Attack path: compromise machine with RBCD write rights, grant yourself delegation, request service ticket as Domain Admin
Harden: inventory TrustedForDelegation, msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo, msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity; justify or remove each

example.code:
Get-ADComputer -Filter {TrustedForDelegation -eq $true} | Select Name
Get-ADUser -Filter * -Properties msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo | Where {$_.'msDS-AllowedToDelegateTo'} | Select Name
example.walkthrough: Every delegation entry is an attack path someone has used. Justify or remove each one in your lab.

pitfalls: 'We need unconstrained delegation' — almost never true; push for constrained
Machine accounts with RBCD rights and no owner
No alerting on delegation configuration changes
lessons.try_it: Inventory delegation in your lab; remove one unjustified entry with documentation.

lessons.title: GPO Security Baselines
concepts: Start from Microsoft Security Compliance Toolkit baselines: import, compare, customize with documented exceptions
Harden: password/lockout policy, user rights assignment, security options (SMB signing, LAN Manager level), audit policy
Never pile everything into Default Domain Policy — purpose-named GPOs at the right scope stay manageable
Back up GPOs (Backup-GPO) before changes; a bad security GPO replicates domain-wide instantly

example.code:
Backup-GPO -All -Path C:\GPOBackups\pre-hardening
# Then compare with Policy Analyzer:
# baseline vs current -> review deltas
example.walkthrough: Treat GPOs like code: backed up, reviewed, change-controlled. The baseline diff is your hardening roadmap.

pitfalls: Editing Default Domain Policy directly — one mistake, domain-wide, no easy undo
Maximum-security settings untested — disabling NTLM breaks legacy apps silently
No backup before changes
lessons.try_it: Back up all lab GPOs and diff against the Microsoft baseline.

lessons.title: GPO Precedence and Troubleshooting
concepts: LSDOU order: Local, Site, Domain, OU — later wins; Enforced and Block Inheritance override deliberately
Security/WMI filtering scopes targets — correct link plus wrong filter applies to nobody
Tools: gpresult /r, gpresult /h, Event 1500-1502, Resultant Set of Policy
Loopback processing (merge/replace) for kiosk/RDS where computer policy shapes user sessions

example.code:
gpresult /r /scope:computer
gpresult /h C:\temp\gpo.html
# Winning GPO for a setting: check 'Winning GPO' column
example.walkthrough: When a setting does not apply, walk LSDOU with gpresult: find where it should win, then check link, filter, and replication.

pitfalls: Forgetting replication delay — new GPOs need gpupdate /force plus patience
Block Inheritance surprises — document every use
WMI filter typos silently excluding everyone
lessons.try_it: Create a test GPO, link it, and verify with gpresult that it wins.

lessons.title: GPO Attack Surface
concepts: GPOs are high-value targets: modify one GPO, own every machine it touches — delegate GPO edit rights tightly
Dangerous settings attackers love: logon scripts, scheduled tasks, software install, registry pushes — all are persistence vectors
Monitor: Event 5136 (directory change) on GPO objects, SYSVOL file auditing, alert on new GPO links at domain root
AGPM (Advanced Group Policy Management) adds change control: checkout, review, approve — treat GPOs like production code

example.code:
# Who can edit GPOs? (should be a tiny list)
Get-GPO -All | ForEach { Get-GPPermission -Guid $_.Id -All | Where {$_.Permission -eq 'GpoEdit'} }
example.walkthrough: Audit who can edit each GPO in your lab. Every name on that list can push code to every domain computer — make sure the list is short and justified.

pitfalls: Domain Users with GPO edit rights — game over if phished
Logon scripts in GPOs with no integrity monitoring
No alerting on GPO modifications
lessons.try_it: List GPO editors in your lab; remove or justify each entry.

lessons.title: Hardening Authentication Policies
concepts: Authentication Policies and Silos (2012R2+): restrict where privileged accounts can authenticate — DA credentials only valid on DCs and PAWs
Protected Users group: no NTLM, no DES/RC4, no delegation, TGT lifetime capped at 4h — apply to all privileged accounts
Tiered admin model via GPO: Tier 0 (DCs) only administrable from PAWs with Tier 0 creds; GPOs enforce the boundaries
LAPS: unique local admin passwords per machine, rotated automatically, readable only by authorized helpdesk

example.code:
# Protected Users membership (all privileged accounts belong here):
Add-ADGroupMember 'Protected Users' -Members admin1,admin2
# Verify LAPS password retrieval:
Get-LapsADPassword -Identity WS-042 | Select Password
example.walkthrough: Protected Users plus Authentication Silos converts 'DA creds work everywhere' into 'DA creds work only on DCs from PAWs' — lateral movement dies at the boundary.

pitfalls: Privileged accounts NOT in Protected Users — the group only helps members
LAPS deployed but helpdesk cannot read passwords — they will disable it
Authentication silos misconfigured locking admins out — test in lab first
lessons.try_it: Add your lab admin accounts to Protected Users and verify logon still works.

lessons.title: Replication Topology and KCC
concepts: AD replication is multi-master: every DC is writable (except RODCs); changes converge via replication, not a primary/secondary push
KCC (Knowledge Consistency Checker) auto-builds the replication topology: ring topology within a site (15s), hub-spoke between sites per schedule
Connection objects define replication partners; the ISTG picks bridgehead servers for inter-site replication
repadmin is the diagnostic core: /showrepl (status), /replsummary (health), /queue (backlog), /syncall (force)

example.code:
repadmin /replsummary
repadmin /showrepl DC01
repadmin /queue DC01
# Healthy: 0 errors, deltas < 60s intra-site
example.walkthrough: Run /replsummary weekly and trend it: today's clean output is tomorrow's baseline for detecting replication decay before users notice.

pitfalls: Ignoring /replsummary errors 'because everything works' — replication debt compounds
Manual connection objects fighting the KCC — let KCC work unless you have a reason
No monitoring of replication health between maintenance windows
lessons.try_it: Run repadmin /replsummary in your lab and document every error until it is clean.

lessons.title: Sites, Subnets, and Service Location
concepts: AD Sites map physical topology: subnets belong to sites, sites link via site links with cost/schedule/replication interval
Clients find DCs via DNS SRV records weighted by site: correct site assignment means logons stay local and fast
Subnet objects must cover every client IP range — unmapped subnets get random site assignment and slow logons
Site link bridging, costs, and schedules control inter-site replication traffic — design for your WAN, not the defaults

example.code:
# Verify client site assignment:
nltest /dsgetsite
# List subnets missing from sites: compare DHCP scopes vs AD subnets
Get-ADReplicationSubnet -Filter * | Select Name,Site
example.walkthrough: Audit every subnet in your environment against AD Sites: each unmapped subnet is slow logons and helpdesk tickets you can prevent today.

pitfalls: Subnets missing from AD Sites — the #1 cause of 'slow logons' mysteries
Default site link schedule replicating huge changes over slow WAN at noon
No site for a new office — clients authenticate across the WAN
lessons.try_it: Run nltest /dsgetsite from several locations; fix any wrong-site assignments.

lessons.title: Lingering Objects and USN Issues
concepts: Lingering objects: deleted objects that resurrect on DCs offline past tombstone lifetime (default 180 days) — strict replication consistency prevents reanimation
USN rollback: restoring a DC from snapshot without proper procedure causes permanent, undetectable divergence — never snapshot-restore a DC casually
repadmin /removelingeringobjects cleans them; the real fix is monitoring replication so no DC exceeds tombstone lifetime
Event 1388/1988 (lingering), 2095 (USN rollback): know these IDs — they signal replication integrity failure

example.code:
repadmin /removelingeringobjects DC01 <GUID> DC=corp,DC=lab /advisory_mode
# Advisory first! Then without /advisory_mode to actually remove.
example.walkthrough: Advisory mode first, always: see what would be removed before removing it. Lingering object cleanup without a backup is a resume-generating event.

pitfalls: Deleting lingering objects without advisory mode or backup
Snapshot-restoring DCs like member servers — USN rollback is forever
DC offline > tombstone lifetime then rejoined without cleanup
lessons.try_it: Check tombstone lifetime and oldest DC offline duration in your lab.

lessons.title: Backup, Restore, and Disaster Recovery
concepts: System State backup captures AD: use Windows Server Backup or AD-aware agents; test restores regularly or you have no backup
Authoritative vs non-authoritative restore: non-authoritative (normal) takes current replication state; authoritative (ntdsutil) forces your restored objects to win
AD Recycle Bin: restores deleted objects with attributes intact — enable it before you need it (forest functional level 2008R2+)
DC recovery priority: seize FSMO roles if holders are lost, clean metadata of dead DCs, rebuild — document the runbook before the disaster

example.code:
# Enable AD Recycle Bin (one-way door, plan it):
Enable-ADOptionalFeature 'Recycle Bin Feature' -Scope ForestOrConfigurationSet -Target corp.lab
# Restore a deleted user:
Get-ADObject -Filter {displayName -eq 'Jane Doe'} -IncludeDeletedObjects | Restore-ADObject
example.walkthrough: Enable the Recycle Bin in your lab today and practice a delete-restore cycle. The first time you need it must not be the first time you use it.

pitfalls: No tested restore — untested backups are Schrödinger's backups
Authoritative restore without understanding USN impact — can resurrect deleted objects domain-wide
Dead DC metadata left in AD — replication and auth errors for months
lessons.try_it: Practice: delete a test user, restore via Recycle Bin, verify attributes.

lessons.title: DNS for Active Directory
concepts: AD cannot function without DNS: DC location via SRV records (_ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs), Kerberos, and Group Policy all depend on it
AD-integrated zones replicate through AD replication (no zone transfers needed) and support secure dynamic updates
Aging and scavenging prevent stale records: configure no-refresh + refresh intervals, then enable scavenging on the zone and server
DNSSEC signs zones against spoofing; DNS policies can split-brain views — know when each is worth the complexity

example.code:
# Verify DC SRV records:
nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.lab
# Check scavenging config:
Get-DnsServerZone -Name corp.lab | Select Aging,AvailForScavengeTime
example.walkthrough: If SRV records are wrong or missing, nothing in AD works right. Verify them after every DNS change — they are the foundation everything else stands on.

pitfalls: Non-AD DNS hosting the AD zone without dynamic update support — SRV records go stale
Scavenging misconfigured deleting valid records — set intervals carefully
Single DNS server for the domain — DNS is a single point of failure for AD
lessons.try_it: Verify all DC SRV records resolve correctly in your lab.

lessons.title: Secure Dynamic Updates and DNS Security
concepts: Secure-only dynamic updates: only authenticated machines update their own records — prevents DNS hijacking via unauthenticated updates
DNS cache poisoning defense: randomized source ports, transaction IDs, and response rate limiting; DNSSEC for cryptographic assurance
DNS logging (analytical logs) reveals tunneling and exfiltration: monitor for abnormal query volumes, long labels, rare record types
Split DNS: internal vs external views — never expose internal AD DNS structure to the internet

example.code:
# Enforce secure-only updates:
Set-DnsServerPrimaryZone -Name corp.lab -DynamicUpdate Secure
# Enable DNS analytical logging for threat hunting
example.walkthrough: Flip one zone to secure-only in the lab and watch what breaks: anything updating DNS without domain credentials was a finding, not a feature.

pitfalls: Nonsecure-and-secure updates 'for compatibility' — the compatibility is with attackers
AD DNS zone exposed to the internet — internal structure leaked
No DNS query logging — tunneling invisible
lessons.try_it: Enable DNS analytical logging in the lab; baseline normal query patterns.

lessons.title: DHCP Security and Reliability
concepts: DHCP is unauthenticated by design: rogue servers, starvation attacks, and option injection are the threat model
Defenses: DHCP snooping on switches (trusted vs untrusted ports), authorized servers in AD, 802.1X for port-level control
Reliability: split scopes or failover (hot standby / load balance) — a single DHCP server is a single point of failure for booting clients
Audit: reconcile scopes against IPAM; unknown leases are either new devices or rogue activity — investigate

example.code:
# Authorize DHCP in AD (rogue prevention):
Add-DhcpServerInDc -DnsName dhcp01.corp.lab -IPAddress 10.0.1.10
# Failover config:
Add-DhcpServerv4Failover -Name CLU-FO -PartnerServer dhcp02.corp.lab -ScopeId 10.0.1.0 -LoadBalancePercent 50
example.walkthrough: Authorize your DHCP servers and enable snooping on the lab switches. Then plug in a rogue DHCP server and watch the defenses work — or find the gap before an attacker does.

pitfalls: Unauthorized DHCP servers — AD authorization exists for this reason
Single DHCP server, no failover — one failure, no new clients
No snooping on access switches — rogue server plugs in anywhere
lessons.try_it: Verify DHCP authorization state and failover config in your lab.

lessons.title: DNS/DHCP Troubleshooting
concepts: DNS failure modes: resolution fails (server down?), wrong answers (stale/poisoned?), slow (forwarders?), AD-specific (SRV missing?)
DHCP failure modes: no address (server down? scope exhausted? relay missing?), wrong address (rogue server?), no options (misconfigured scope?)
Toolchain: nslookup/dig, ipconfig /displaydns, Get-DnsServerDiagnostics; ipconfig /release /renew, DHCP server logs, switch snooping tables
Always verify the client config first: wrong DNS server on the NIC explains half of all 'AD is broken' tickets

example.code:
ipconfig /all          # what DNS/DHCP is the client actually using?
nslookup corp.lab       # does the configured DNS answer?
Get-DhcpServerv4ScopeStatistics  # scope exhaustion?
example.walkthrough: Half of AD emergencies are client network config. ipconfig /all before anything else — thirty seconds that prevents thirty minutes.

pitfalls: Troubleshooting AD before checking the client's DNS settings
Forgetting DHCP relay (ip helper) on VLANs without local DHCP
Scope exhaustion discovered during an outage instead of monitoring
lessons.try_it: Document the DHCP/DNS verification sequence as a runbook.

lessons.title: AD Module Essentials
concepts: Import-Module ActiveDirectory: the foundation — Get-ADUser/Computer/Group/OU/Object cover 90% of daily tasks
-Filter vs -LDAPFilter: -Filter is PowerShell syntax, -LDAPFilter is raw LDAP; LDAP filters are faster for complex queries
-Properties: default property sets are minimal — always specify what you need (never -Properties * in production; it is slow)
Pipeline discipline: filter left (at the DC) with -Filter/-SearchBase, format right — never pull 50k objects to filter locally

example.code: Get-ADUser -Filter {Enabled -eq $true} -SearchBase 'OU=Users,DC=corp,DC=lab' -Properties LastLogonDate,PasswordLastSet | Select Name,LastLogonDate
example.walkthrough: Filter at the source every time: -SearchBase and -Filter run on the DC; Where-Object runs on your machine after pulling everything. At scale this is the difference between seconds and timeouts.

pitfalls: -Properties * in scripts — slow and breaks when schema changes
Filtering 100k users with Where-Object instead of -Filter
No -SearchBase — querying the whole domain for OU-scoped data
lessons.try_it: Write a one-liner listing disabled users with last logon dates, filtered at the DC.

lessons.title: Enumeration Like an Attacker (to Defend)
concepts: BloodHound/ADExplorer mindset: map attack paths — who can reach Domain Admins via group nesting, ACLs, and sessions?
Key queries: unconstrained delegation, AdminCount=1 accounts, stale privileged logons, GPO edit rights, LAPS coverage gaps
ACL auditing: Get-ACL on AD objects reveals WriteDacl/GenericAll rights — the quietest privilege escalation paths
Run attacker tooling in the lab (PingCastle, Purple Knight) to score your own domain before adversaries do

example.code:
# Stale privileged accounts (no logon 90+ days, still enabled):
$cutoff=(Get-Date).AddDays(-90)
Get-ADUser -Filter {Enabled -eq $true -and AdminCount -eq 1} -Properties LastLogonDate | Where {$_.LastLogonDate -lt $cutoff} | Select Name,LastLogonDate
example.walkthrough: Schedule the attacker-view queries monthly: the report that shows your exposure shrinking over time is the most persuasive security metric you can bring to leadership.

pitfalls: Running scans but never remediating — findings without fixes are liability documentation
Scanning production without approval — get written authorization first
Trusting a clean scan — tools miss custom misconfigurations
lessons.try_it: Run one attacker-view query in your lab and remediate the top finding.

lessons.title: Bulk Operations Safely
concepts: Bulk user provisioning: CSV + New-ADUser loop with -WhatIf first, then a pilot batch, then full run with transcript logging
Disable (never delete) departing users immediately; move to a Disabled OU that strips group memberships via script
Password operations: use -AccountPassword (SecureString), enforce the policy, never hardcode — read from a vault
Every bulk script gets: WhatIf pass, pilot (5 objects), full run with Start-Transcript, and a rollback plan

example.walkthrough: -WhatIf is not optional for bulk operations: the pilot batch of 5 catches the CSV column mismatch before it creates 500 broken accounts.

pitfalls: Bulk scripts without -WhatIf pilot — 500 malformed accounts in seconds
Deleting instead of disabling — destroys forensics and rehire paths
Passwords in plaintext in scripts — committed to the repo forever
lessons.try_it: Write a bulk-disable script with WhatIf + transcript for departing users.

lessons.title: Constrained Endpoints (JEA)
concepts: Just Enough Administration: expose only specific cmdlets with specific parameters to helpdesk — no full admin rights needed
Role capability files define what; session configuration files define who — the endpoint enforces both
Example: helpdesk can Reset-ADAccountPassword and Unlock-ADAccount, only for non-privileged OUs, with full transcription
JEA kills standing privilege: the helpdesk never holds Domain Admin, yet can do their job

example.code:
# Register a helpdesk endpoint (on the server):
New-PSSessionConfigurationFile -Path .\Helpdesk.pssc -SessionType RestrictedRemoteServer
# Role capability allows only:
# VisibleCmdlets = 'Reset-ADAccountPassword','Unlock-ADAccount','Get-ADUser'
Register-PSSessionConfiguration -Name Helpdesk -Path .\Helpdesk.pssc
example.walkthrough: JEA is the answer to 'helpdesk needs admin rights': they get exactly the cmdlets they need, on exactly the OUs they support, with every action transcribed.

pitfalls: JEA roles copied from the internet without scoping to your OUs
No transcription — JEA without logging is just obscurity
Over-broad VisibleCmdlets defeating the purpose
lessons.try_it: Design a JEA role for password resets scoped to a single OU.

lessons.title: System State Backups
concepts: System State captures AD DS, SYSVOL, registry, and boot files — the minimum viable AD backup; file-level backups of ntds.dit are NOT supported
Use Windows Server Backup or AD-aware enterprise agents; verify backup completion in event logs, not just the agent console
Backup at least two DCs per domain, stored offsite/offline — ransomware encrypts online backups first
Document bare-metal recovery media location and BitLocker keys before the disaster, not during

example.code:
wbadmin start systemstatebackup -backuptarget:E:
# Verify:
wbadmin get versions
# Event: Microsoft-Windows-Backup Operational log, Event 4 (success)
example.walkthrough: A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup. Schedule quarterly restore tests to an isolated lab and document the results.

pitfalls: File-copying ntds.dit while AD runs — corrupt and unrestorable
Backups on the same SAN as production — one ransomware event takes both
No documented restore procedure — the runbook is written during the fire
lessons.try_it: Verify your lab's System State backup completed this week and document where it lives.

lessons.title: Authoritative Restore Deep Dive
concepts: Non-authoritative: restored DC takes current replication state (normal for DC rebuild) — restored objects stay deleted if deleted elsewhere
Authoritative (ntdsutil): marks restored objects with higher version numbers so they replicate OUT and overwrite — use for accidental mass deletion
Granular: restore specific OUs/objects authoritatively without full-forest impact — the scalpel vs the sledgehammer
Procedure order matters: boot DSRM, restore System State, ntdsutil authoritative restore, reboot normal, verify replication

example.code:
ntdsutil
activate instance ntds
authoritative restore
restore subtree "OU=Sales,DC=corp,DC=lab"
quit
# Then reboot normally and monitor repadmin
example.walkthrough: Practice the full authoritative restore in an isolated lab annually: DSRM password, backup media, ntdsutil syntax, verification steps. The procedure has sharp edges you want to meet in practice.

pitfalls: Authoritative restore of the wrong subtree — resurrects objects intentionally deleted elsewhere
Forgetting DSRM password — set and vault it now
Restoring a DC older than tombstone lifetime — creates lingering objects
lessons.try_it: Write the authoritative restore runbook for one OU, including DSRM access.

lessons.title: AD Recycle Bin Operations
concepts: Recycle Bin preserves deleted objects WITH attributes (group memberships intact) — without it, restores lose everything but the name
Enablement is one-way and forest-wide (2008R2+ functional level); enable it during peacetime, never during the incident
Two stages: Deleted Objects (restorable, default 180 days) then Recycled (tombstone); Restore-ADObject or ADAC GUI
It does not protect against: malicious admin purges beyond retention, schema changes, or configuration partition damage — still need backups

example.code:
# One-way enablement (plan first):
Enable-ADOptionalFeature 'Recycle Bin Feature' -Scope ForestOrConfigurationSet -Target corp.lab
# Restore:
Get-ADObject -Filter {displayName -eq 'Jane Doe'} -IncludeDeletedObjects | Restore-ADObject
example.walkthrough: Enable the Recycle Bin this week and drill a delete-restore cycle. It converts most 'I deleted the wrong OU' incidents from disasters into 5-minute fixes.

pitfalls: Assuming Recycle Bin replaces backups — it does not cover all partitions or malice
Never testing restore — the first real use should not be the first use
Retention shorter than your incident discovery time
lessons.try_it: Enable Recycle Bin in the lab; practice delete and restore with attribute verification.

lessons.title: Forest Recovery Planning
concepts: Forest recovery is the nuclear option: all DCs rebuilt from backup in isolation, seized roles, metadata cleanup — rehearse it, do not improvise it
Microsoft's forest recovery guide is the playbook: follow it step by step; deviations create USN and replication chaos
Recovery priority: PDC emulator first (time + password authority), then RID/PDC-adjacent roles, then the rest
The real deliverable is the tested runbook: roles, backups, media, passwords, network isolation plan, communication plan

example.code:
Forest recovery phases:
  1. Isolate & assess (stop replication chaos)
  2. Recover first DC from backup (non-auth, isolated)
  3. Seize all FSMO roles to it
  4. Clean metadata of lost DCs
  5. Rebuild remaining DCs fresh, repromote
  6. Verify end-to-end, reconnect
example.walkthrough: Print the forest recovery runbook and store it offline: during a real forest disaster, the wiki may be down too.

pitfalls: No offline copy of the runbook — the plan lives on the systems that are down
Skipping the rehearsal — first-time forest recovery under pressure fails
Forgetting service accounts and app dependencies in the recovery order
lessons.try_it: Draft the one-page forest recovery contact/roles sheet for your environment.

lessons.title: Entra Connect Sync Models
concepts: Password Hash Sync (PHS): hashes sync to Entra ID; auth happens in cloud; simplest and most resilient — Microsoft's recommended default
Pass-Through Authentication (PTA): passwords validated against on-prem DCs via lightweight agents; no hash in cloud but on-prem dependency
Federation (AD FS): full control and SSO customization at the cost of maximum infrastructure complexity — use only when PHS/PTA cannot meet requirements
One sync method per domain: choose deliberately, document why, and know the failover behavior of your choice

example.code:
# Check sync configuration:
Get-ADSyncScheduler
# Staging mode check (should be false on active, true on standby):
Get-ADSyncScheduler | Select StagingModeEnabled
example.walkthrough: Most organizations should use PHS: it survives on-prem outages and is the simplest to operate. Choose PTA or federation only for specific documented requirements.

pitfalls: Federation 'for control' without a requirement — maximum complexity, minimal benefit
No staging-mode standby server — single point of sync failure
Syncing everything instead of scoping OUs — service accounts and break-glass in the cloud
lessons.try_it: Document your environment's sync method and the reason it was chosen.

lessons.title: Seamless SSO and Conditional Access
concepts: Seamless SSO: Kerberos-based silent sign-in for domain-joined machines — computer account decrypts the ticket, no password prompt
Conditional Access is the policy engine: signals (user, device, location, risk) → decisions (allow, require MFA, block)
Hybrid join states: Hybrid Entra Joined devices bridge both worlds — verify join state before writing CA policies against it
Legacy auth blocking: disable basic/legacy auth via CA — it bypasses MFA entirely and is the attacker's favorite

example.code:
# Verify Hybrid Join:
dsregcmd /status   # AzureAdJoined: YES, DomainJoined: YES
# Check SSO Kerberos decryption account:
Get-ADUser -Filter {Name -like 'AZUREADSSO*'}
example.walkthrough: Block legacy auth in Conditional Access this week: it is the single highest-leverage identity hardening action in hybrid environments.

pitfalls: CA policies in report-only forever — enforce after the pilot proves safety
Seamless SSO misconfigured, users prompted anyway — check the Kerberos account
Break-glass accounts caught by CA blocks — exclude them from every policy
lessons.try_it: Run dsregcmd /status on a workstation; verify Hybrid Join state.

lessons.title: Privileged Identity Management
concepts: PIM converts standing admin into just-in-time: eligible assignments activated with MFA, reason, and time limit — then auto-revoked
Apply to both Entra roles and Azure resources; on-prem analog: JEA + time-bound group membership
Access reviews: recurring certification that eligible admins still need eligibility — removes entitlement creep
Alert on: activations outside hours, mass activations, PIM configuration changes

example.code:
# Time-bound group membership (on-prem analog):
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Temp-Admins' -Members $user -MemberTimeToLive (New-TimeSpan -Hours 4)
example.walkthrough: Every hour of standing privilege is an hour of unnecessary risk. PIM turns 'always admin' into 'admin for the approved hour.'

pitfalls: Eligible but never reviewed — PIM without access reviews is decoration
Break-glass excluded from PIM but also from monitoring
Activation without MFA requirement
lessons.try_it: List who holds eligible (not active) admin roles; verify each still needs it.

lessons.title: Hybrid Attack Paths
concepts: Sync account compromise: the ADSync service account has broad read (and write-back, if enabled) — protect it like a DA
DC-to-cloud pivots: attackers with DCSync can forge the PHS hashes; cloud admins with sync rights can push back to on-prem with writeback
Seamless SSO account: the AZUREADSSO computer account's Kerberos key — if stolen, forge SSO tickets (mitigate: rotate via the documented procedure)
Defense: tier the sync servers as Tier 0, monitor sync configuration changes, alert on DCSync (Event 4662 with replication GUIDs)

example.code:
# Protect the sync account:
# - Dedicated account, 25+ char password, in protected OU
# - Deny interactive logon
# - Monitor 4662 for DCSync replication attempts
example.walkthrough: The sync server is a Tier 0 asset: it bridges both identity planes. Harden it like a domain controller, because to an attacker it is one.

pitfalls: Sync server treated as a regular member server
Writeback enabled without a documented need
No monitoring for DCSync — the quietest domain takeover
lessons.try_it: Verify your sync server's tiering and the sync account's protections.

lessons.title: Audit Policy Design
concepts: Audit what matters: logon events (4624/4625), account management (4720/4728/4732/4756), directory changes (5136), policy changes (4719)
Advanced Audit Policy (via GPO) replaces basic auditing: granular subcategories, no confusing overlaps
Balance volume vs value: audit success+failure for critical categories; failure-only where volume is crushing
Centralize: Windows Event Forwarding to a collector or SIEM — local logs are the first thing attackers clear

example.code:
# Enable via GPO: Advanced Audit Policy Configuration
# Verify effective policy:
auditpol /get /category:* | Select-String 'Logon','Account Management'
example.walkthrough: Design auditing from the investigation backward: 'When the incident comes, which events will I need?' Enable those now.

pitfalls: Basic + Advanced auditing mixed — conflicting, confusing results
No centralization — attacker clears the local log, evidence gone
Auditing everything — volume buries the signal
lessons.try_it: Document which event IDs your audit policy captures and why.

lessons.title: Reading Authentication Logs
concepts: 4624 anatomy: Logon Type (2 interactive, 3 network, 10 RDP), source IP/workstation, account name — the story of every auth
4625 failures: sub-status codes distinguish bad password (0xC000006A) from disabled (0xC0000072) from locked (0xC0000234)
4768/4769/4771: the Kerberos trail — correlate with 4624s to separate Kerberos from NTLM auth
Baseline normal first: service accounts log on at odd hours legitimately — know your normal before hunting abnormal

example.code:
# Failed logons by user (hunt password spraying):
Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Security'; ID=4625} | Group-Object -Property {$_.Properties[5].Value} | Sort Count -Descending | Select -First 10
example.walkthrough: Learn the sub-status codes cold: 0xC000006A vs 0xC0000234 is the difference between 'spraying' and 'already locked' — your response differs entirely.

pitfalls: Treating all 4625s equally — the sub-status is the diagnosis
No baseline — every service account looks like an anomaly
Ignoring Logon Type — type 3 vs type 10 changes the story
lessons.try_it: Pull last week's 4625s; categorize by sub-status code.

lessons.title: SIEM Detection Engineering
concepts: Detections as code: each rule has a hypothesis, logic, threshold, tuning history, and runbook — versioned like software
High-value AD detections: DCSync (4662+GUIDs), Kerberoasting (4769 volume+RC4), golden ticket (4768 lifetime anomaly), new DA (4728 to Domain Admins)
Tune with baselines: run every new rule in alert-only for 2 weeks, measure false positives, then promote to paging
Detection debt: review quarterly — stale rules generate noise, noise gets ignored, ignored noise hides breaches

example.code:
Detection spec template:
  NAME: Possible Kerberoasting
  LOGIC: 4769 count > 100/hour per source AND encryption = 0x17
  BASELINE: max normal 12/hour
  ACTION: isolate host, rotate targeted service passwords
  TUNING LOG: 2026-08-01: threshold 50->100 (backup server FP)
example.walkthrough: Every detection needs a runbook: an alert without a documented response is just anxiety with a timestamp.

pitfalls: Rules without baselines — alert storms on day one
No tuning log — the same false positive fires for a year
Detections without runbooks — analysts improvise under pressure
lessons.try_it: Write one detection spec (with runbook) for an AD attack technique.

lessons.title: Threat Hunting in AD
concepts: Hunting is hypothesis-driven: 'I hypothesize Kerberoasting occurred; I will look for 4769 volume anomalies' — not 'let me browse logs'
Start with intel and crown jewels: what would attackers want here, and what would it look like in our logs?
Time-box hunts (half-day sprints) with documented hypotheses, data sources, findings, and follow-ups
Feed results back: confirmed techniques become detections; disproven hypotheses refine the threat model

example.code:
Hunt card:
  HYPOTHESIS: Attackers used BloodHound-style recon
  LOOK FOR: 4662 bulk object reads, LDAP queries from non-admin hosts
  DATA: DC security logs, 30 days
  TIMEBOX: 4 hours
  OUTCOME: [findings] -> [new detection or closed]
example.walkthrough: A hunt that finds nothing still has value if the hypothesis was sound — you have verified a negative. Document it either way.

pitfalls: Aimless log browsing — hunting without hypotheses is sightseeing
No timebox — hunts expand to fill all available time
Findings not converted to detections — the next hunter repeats your work
lessons.try_it: Write one hunt card for an AD technique and execute it in the lab.

lessons.title: The Tiered Administration Model
concepts: Tier 0: domain controllers, AD, PKI — the keys to the kingdom; Tier 1: servers and apps; Tier 2: workstations — compromise flows upward, so protect downward
The iron rule: higher tiers never log on to lower tiers — Tier 0 creds never touch a workstation, enforced technically not by policy memo
Credential separation: distinct accounts per tier (admin-T0, admin-T1, admin-T2) — one human, three identities, zero crossover
PAWs (Privileged Access Workstations): hardened, dedicated machines for Tier 0 work — the only place Tier 0 creds exist

example.code:
Tier model:
  Tier 0: DCs, AD, Entra Connect, PKI  <- PAW only, Tier 0 creds
  Tier 1: Member servers, apps     <- jump host, Tier 1 creds
  Tier 2: Workstations              <- Tier 2 creds
  NEVER: Tier 0 cred on Tier 2 machine
example.walkthrough: Draw your environment's tiers this week and mark every place the model is violated: each violation is a lateral-movement highway. Fix the cheapest one first.

pitfalls: Tiering on paper only — no technical enforcement, just a memo
Same password across tiers — one phish compromises all tiers
PAWs that also browse the web — a PAW with internet is a workstation
lessons.try_it: Map your admin accounts to tiers; identify every crossover violation.

lessons.title: LAPS Deployment and Operations
concepts: LAPS: every machine gets a unique, rotated local admin password — kills lateral movement via shared local creds
Windows LAPS (built-in): stores in AD/Entra, policy-driven rotation, readable by authorized principals only
Operationalize: helpdesk retrieval workflow (who can read, audited), break-glass for offline machines, monitor for LAPS-not-installed
Legacy LAPS vs Windows LAPS: migrate to the built-in version — better crypto, Entra support, active development

example.code:
# Deploy via GPO: enable Windows LAPS, set password length/complexity/age
# Retrieve (authorized only):
Get-LapsADPassword -Identity WS-042
# Audit coverage:
Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties ms-LAPS-Password | Where {!$_.'ms-LAPS-Password'} | Select Name
example.walkthrough: The audit query is the money: every machine without a LAPS password is a lateral-movement stepping stone. Drive that list to zero.

pitfalls: LAPS deployed but nobody can read passwords — helpdesk disables it to work
No audit of retrieval — who read which password when is invisible
Excluding 'special' machines from LAPS — attackers love exceptions
lessons.try_it: Audit LAPS coverage in your lab; get it to 100%.

lessons.title: Just-In-Time Administration
concepts: JIT: privilege exists only for the approved window — standing admin is the risk, JIT is the control
On-prem: time-bound group membership (MemberTimeToLive), PIM for hybrid, approval workflows with reason capture
Every elevation logged with: who, why, what window, what was done — the audit trail is the point
Emergency access: break-glass accounts outside JIT, sealed, monitored, tested quarterly

example.code:
# Time-bound membership (4 hours):
Add-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Server-Admins-JIT' -Members $user -MemberTimeToLive (New-TimeSpan -Hours 4)
# Verify expiry:
Get-ADGroupMember -Identity 'Server-Admins-JIT'
example.walkthrough: Start with one group: convert the most-abused standing admin group to JIT this month. Measure the reduction in standing privilege hours.

pitfalls: JIT without approval workflow — self-service elevation is just admin with extra steps
No expiry verification — 'temporary' memberships that never expire
Break-glass untested — discover it is broken during the emergency
lessons.try_it: Convert one standing admin group to 4-hour JIT in the lab.

lessons.title: Credential Theft Defenses
concepts: LSASS is the target: Credential Guard (VBS isolation), PPL protection, and blocking unsigned drivers raise the cost of dumping
WDigest: disable it (off by default modern, but verify) — it stores plaintext-equivalent passwords in memory
Network defenses: SMB signing required (no relay), LDAP signing/channel binding (no downgrade), RDP Restricted Admin
Assume-breach: even with defenses, plan for credential theft — short lifetimes (Protected Users 4h TGT), tiering, and rapid rotation limit the blast

example.code:
# Verify Credential Guard:
(Get-CimInstance Win32_DeviceGuard).SecurityServicesRunning
# Check WDigest:
Get-ItemProperty 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest' -Name UseLogonCredential
example.walkthrough: Run the verification commands across your fleet: every machine without Credential Guard is a credential-theft waiting room.

pitfalls: WDigest still enabled 'for legacy' with no documented legacy
SMB signing not required — relay attacks welcome
Long-lived creds for privileged accounts — theft has maximum value
lessons.try_it: Audit Credential Guard and WDigest state across your lab machines.

lessons.title: Capstone: AD Defense Lab — Overview
concepts: Your capstone: a hardened Active Directory lab with attack simulation and detection
Break the build into phases: plan, build, secure, validate, document. Each phase maps to domains in this bootcamp
Document as you go — your write-up is the interview artifact that proves senior-level ownership
Done beats perfect: a working system with honest limitations beats an unfinished ambitious one

example.code:
Phase 1: Build a 2-DC lab with proper sites and DNS
Phase 2: Harden: baselines, LAPS, Protected Users, tiering
Phase 3: Attack your own lab (Kerberoasting, delegation) safely
Phase 4: Build detections for each attack in your SIEM
Phase 5: Write the incident response runbook and present findings
example.walkthrough: Treat each phase as a mini-project with a definition of done. Demo each phase working before moving on — integration surprises compound.

pitfalls: Starting to build before writing the plan — an hour of planning saves ten of rework
Skipping documentation until the end — you will forget why decisions were made
Gold-plating phase one while phase four remains untouched
lessons.try_it: Write the one-paragraph project plan: what you will build, in what phases, and what 'done' looks like.

lessons.title: Capstone: Validation and Demo
concepts: Validate every requirement with a test you can show: screenshots, command output, or a live demo
Prepare the 5-minute demo narrative: problem, approach, build, validation, lessons learned
Anticipate questions: know the trade-offs you made and what you would do with more time
Publish the write-up: architecture diagram, build log, validation evidence, reflection

example.code:
Demo script template:
  1. The problem (30s)
  2. Architecture overview (60s)
  3. Live walkthrough (2 min)
  4. Validation evidence (60s)
  5. What I would do next (30s)
example.walkthrough: A demo that only shows the happy path invites the hardest questions. Show one failure mode and how the system handles it — that is what interviewers remember.

pitfalls: Demoing without rehearsing — run it three times end-to-end first
Hiding limitations — name them before you are asked
No architecture diagram — draw the system before you demo it
lessons.try_it: Draft your 5-minute demo script for the capstone project.

lessons.title: AD Security Fundamentals
concepts: Active Directory is the identity plane: compromise AD and you own every joined system — defend it as the highest-value target
Assume-breach mindset: design as if attackers are already inside; focus on limiting blast radius and detecting lateral movement
The kill chain in AD: initial access -> recon -> credential theft -> privilege escalation -> persistence -> objective
Defense layers: harden, monitor, segment, and rehearse — no single control stops a determined attacker

example.code:
Defense layers:
  1. Harden: baselines, LAPS, Protected Users, tiering
  2. Monitor: 4624/4625/4768/4769/4728, SIEM rules
  3. Segment: tier model, PAWs, network isolation
  4. Rehearse: tabletop IR, restore drills
example.walkthrough: Map each layer to a domain in this bootcamp: you are building the full stack, not reading about it.

pitfalls: Treating AD as 'just another server' — it is the trust root for everything
Single control reliance — 'we have MFA so we are fine'
No rehearsal — the first incident is not the time to learn the tools
lessons.try_it: Write the AD kill chain for your lab: pick each phase and name the control that breaks it.

lessons.title: Attack Path Mapping
concepts: Attack paths are graphs: BloodHound maps users -> groups -> computers -> Domain Admins via sessions, ACLs, and group nesting
Shortest path analysis: find the fewest hops from a compromised workstation to DA — that is what attackers optimize
Choke points: identify the 2-3 edges whose removal breaks the most paths (e.g., DA session on a workstation)
Continuously map: paths change with every group change, new system, and GPO edit — map monthly at minimum

example.code:
# Key BloodHound queries (concepts):
# - Shortest path to DA from owned principals
# - Unconstrained delegation computers
# - Admins with sessions on workstations
# Fix the choke points first.
example.walkthrough: Install BloodHound in the lab, collect data, and find the three shortest paths to DA. Each is a remediation ticket.

pitfalls: Collecting BloodHound data but never remediating — a map without action is a souvenir
Running collectors in production without approval
Fixing random findings instead of choke points
lessons.try_it: Document the top 3 attack paths in your lab and the fix for each.

lessons.title: Hardening Priorities
concepts: Prioritize by attacker ROI: credential theft paths first (LSASS, delegation, kerberoasting), then persistence, then everything else
Quick wins week one: LAPS, Protected Users, pre-auth enforcement, stale admin cleanup, SMB signing
Structural month one: tiering, PAWs, authentication silos, GPO baselines, backup testing
Measure: track privileged attack surface metrics monthly — stale admins, unconstrained delegation count, RC4 usage

example.code:
Week 1 checklist:
  [ ] LAPS deployed (100% coverage)
  [ ] Privileged accounts in Protected Users
  [ ] Pre-auth enforced (no exceptions)
  [ ] Stale (>90d) privileged accounts disabled
  [ ] SMB signing required
example.walkthrough: Do the quick wins before the architecture: five week-one controls eliminate the most common attack paths.

pitfalls: Boiling the ocean — trying to fix everything at once
No metrics — cannot prove improvement to leadership
Skipping quick wins for perfect architecture
lessons.try_it: Score your lab against the week-1 checklist; fix the first gap.

lessons.title: Incident Response for AD
concepts: AD incidents are identity incidents: assume credential compromise scope is total until proven otherwise
Containment priorities: isolate affected hosts, disable compromised accounts, block malicious persistence — in that order
Eradication: krbtgt double-rotation for Kerberos compromise, full privileged credential reset, GPO/persistence sweep
Recovery: phased service restoration with enhanced monitoring; the post-incident review must produce process changes

example.code:
AD IR phases:
  1. Detect: SIEM alert / hunt finding
  2. Contain: isolate hosts, disable accounts
  3. Eradicate: rotate krbtgt 2x, reset creds, remove persistence
  4. Recover: restore services, monitor hard
  5. Learn: blameless review, process fixes
example.walkthrough: The krbtgt rotation decision is the hardest call in AD IR: it disrupts auth but kills golden tickets. Pre-authorize the criteria now, not at 2 AM.

pitfalls: Partial credential rotation — rotating some admins leaves the attacker in
Skipping the persistence sweep — the attacker returns next week
No blameless review — the next incident repeats this one
lessons.try_it: Write the one-page AD incident call tree: who decides krbtgt rotation at 2 AM?

lessons.title: AD Reconnaissance Techniques
concepts: Attackers map before they strike: LDAP enumeration, SPN scanning, GPO enumeration, and session discovery reveal the attack surface
Common tools: ADFind, BloodHound collectors, PowerView — learn their signatures to detect them
What recon reveals: privileged users, delegation misconfigurations, GPO weaknesses, and trust relationships
Defend by minimizing: reduce what enumeration returns (permissions, group nesting) and alert on bulk queries

example.code:
# ADFind basics (defender must know attacker tools):
# adfind -f "(objectcategory=person)" -dn
# Detect: 4662 bulk reads from non-admin hosts
example.walkthrough: Run ADFind in your lab against your own domain: everything it shows an unauthenticated user is information you are giving attackers for free.

pitfalls: Not knowing what attackers can see — enumerate your own domain regularly
Blocking recon tools instead of fixing the exposures they reveal
No alerting on bulk LDAP queries
lessons.try_it: Run one enumeration query as a standard user; list what should not be visible.

lessons.title: Hunting with Event Logs
concepts: High-value event IDs: 4624/4625 (logons), 4768/4769/4771 (Kerberos), 4720/4728/4732 (account changes), 5136 (directory changes), 4662 (object access)
Correlate across IDs: a 4728 (added to DA) followed by 4624 type 3 from unusual hosts tells the attack story
Time-travel: build timelines of events per host and per user — attacks are sequences, not single events
Filter the noise: baseline normal service account behavior so anomalies stand out

example.code:
# Timeline for a host (concept):
# 4624 type 3 (network logon) -> 4662 (object reads) ->
# 4769 (service tickets) -> 4728 (privilege grant)
# That sequence is an attack in progress.
example.walkthrough: Pick one host and build a 24-hour event timeline. Practice reading the story the events tell together.

pitfalls: Single-event analysis — attacks are sequences
No baselines — everything looks anomalous
Ignoring low-severity events that form the attack chain
lessons.try_it: Build a timeline for one lab host covering logon, Kerberos, and account events.

lessons.title: BloodHound Analysis for Defenders
concepts: BloodHound turns AD into a graph: nodes (users, computers, groups) and edges (MemberOf, AdminTo, CanRDP, GenericAll)
Defender queries: shortest paths to DA, kerberoastable users, unconstrained delegation, cross-trust attack paths
Remediation prioritization: fix edges that appear in the most attack paths first (choke points)
Continuous: re-collect after every change — new GPO, new group member, new server all create new edges

example.code:
Priority query order:
  1. Shortest path to DA (all owned principals)
  2. Unconstrained delegation nodes
  3. Kerberoastable + AS-REP roastable
  4. Admins with sessions on workstations
example.walkthrough: The graph does not lie: if BloodHound finds a 3-hop path from helpdesk to DA, attackers will too. Fix the graph, not just the symptoms.

pitfalls: One-time BloodHound run — the graph changes constantly
Collecting without remediating
Ignoring cross-domain trust edges
lessons.try_it: Run the four priority queries in your lab; ticket the top choke point.

lessons.title: Threat Hunting Queries
concepts: KQL/SPL for AD: craft queries for Kerberoasting (4769 volume + RC4), DCSync (4662 + replication GUIDs), password spraying (4625 patterns)
Hunt hypotheses: 'I believe X happened; I expect to see Y in the logs' — hunts without hypotheses are browsing
Encode hunts as detections: every successful hunt should produce or refine a SIEM rule
Hunt regularly: weekly 2-hour sessions beat quarterly week-long efforts

example.code:
# Kerberoasting hunt (Splunk-style):
# index=dc EventCode=4769 Ticket_Encryption_Type=0x17
# | stats count by TargetUserName, IpAddress | where count > 50
example.walkthrough: Write the query, run it against last week's logs, and document what you find — even 'nothing' is a result worth recording.

pitfalls: Hunts without hypotheses — aimless log diving
Findings not converted to detections
Hunting only after incidents — hunt proactively
lessons.try_it: Write and execute one hunt query in your lab this week.

lessons.title: Kerberos Armoring and FAST
concepts: Flexible Authentication Secure Tunneling (FAST): armors Kerberos exchanges against offline attacks — deploy where supported
Compound identity: FAST binds the user's identity with the machine's, defeating credential forwarding
Enforcement: 'Require FAST' via GPO/KDC policy — audit mode first to find clients that break
Part of the crypto-agility story alongside AES and RC4 removal

example.code:
# Check FAST support:
# GPO: Computer Config -> Policies -> Admin Templates -> System -> Kerberos
# 'Require FAST' -> audit first, then enforce
example.walkthrough: Enable FAST in audit mode in the lab; review which clients fail before enforcing.

pitfalls: Enforcing without audit — legacy clients break silently
Assuming FAST replaces other hardening — it complements, not replaces
No client inventory before rollout
lessons.try_it: Check FAST readiness in your lab environment.

lessons.title: GPO Disaster Recovery
concepts: GPO backups are not optional: Backup-GPO on schedule, versioned, stored offline — ransomware encrypts SYSVOL too
Recovery scenarios: single GPO restore (Import-GPO), full SYSVOL restore, domain-wide GPO rebuild from documentation
Test restores: import a backed-up GPO to a test OU quarterly and verify settings apply
Document the GPO inventory: every GPO's purpose, owner, and link targets — rebuildable from paper if needed

example.code:
# Scheduled GPO backup:
Backup-GPO -All -Path "\\backup\gpo\$(Get-Date -Format yyyyMMdd)"
# Keep 30 days; alert on failure
example.walkthrough: Automate the backup this week: a scheduled task, a network path, and an alert on failure. Future-you will be grateful.

pitfalls: Backups on the same server as AD — one failure takes both
Never testing the restore — Import-GPO surprises await
No GPO inventory — rebuilding from memory
lessons.try_it: Set up scheduled GPO backups with failure alerting.

lessons.title: Monitoring Replication at Scale
concepts: Beyond repadmin: SCOM, Datadog, or custom scripts trending /replsummary over time — point-in-time checks miss decay
Alert thresholds: any replication error, queue > 100, delta > 1h intra-site — page, do not email
Dashboard: per-DC health, oldest backup age, tombstone lifetime countdown for offline DCs
The goal: detect replication issues in minutes, not at the next user complaint

example.code:
# Trending script (concept):
# repadmin /replsummary /csv -> parse -> push to monitoring
# Alert: errors > 0 OR max delta > 3600s
example.walkthrough: Build the trending script this month: today's manual check becomes tomorrow's automated alert.

pitfalls: Manual checks only — decay goes unnoticed for weeks
Alerts to email nobody reads
No tombstone-lifetime tracking for offline DCs
lessons.try_it: Design the replication dashboard: what 5 metrics matter most?

lessons.title: DNSSEC Deployment
concepts: DNSSEC signs DNS data cryptographically: resolvers validate that responses are authentic and untampered
Deployment: sign zones (key ceremonies), publish DS records to parent, configure validators — plan key rollovers
AD-integrated zones support DNSSEC signing; validate the operational overhead before committing
Even without full DNSSEC, understand it: interviewers ask, and it frames all DNS security discussions

example.code:
# Check DNSSEC validation:
# nslookup -type=DNSKEY corp.lab
# Resolve-DnsName -DnssecOk corp.lab
example.walkthrough: Lab it first: sign a test zone, break the signature deliberately, and watch validation fail — that is the security property working.

pitfalls: Deploying without key-rollover planning — expired keys break resolution
Assuming DNSSEC encrypts — it authenticates, not encrypts
No monitoring of validation failures
lessons.try_it: Sign a lab test zone with DNSSEC and verify validation.

lessons.title: AD Reporting Automation
concepts: Scheduled reports: stale accounts, privileged group changes, password expiries, replication health — automated and emailed
Report design: audience-appropriate (executives get trends, engineers get details), actionable (every finding has an owner)
Store history: trending beats snapshots — 'stale admins dropped from 40 to 12 this quarter' proves progress
Alert integration: critical findings (new DA, DCSync) go to SIEM immediately, not in the weekly email

example.walkthrough: Automate one report this month: scheduled, emailed, trended. Reporting that nobody reads is still better than no reporting — but aim for read.

pitfalls: Reports nobody reads — add the trend line that makes them readable
Snapshot-only reporting — trends prove progress
Critical findings in weekly email instead of SIEM alerts
lessons.try_it: Set up one scheduled AD report with emailed output.

lessons.title: Backup Monitoring and Testing
concepts: Monitor backup jobs like production: failed backup = page, not email — a failed backup is a future failed restore
Track backup age per DC: alert if any DC's backup exceeds 24h; aged backups risk tombstone-lifetime issues on restore
Quarterly restore tests with documented results: what worked, what failed, what changed in the runbook
3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offline — ransomware hunts backups first

example.code:
# Backup age check:
wbadmin get versions | Select-String 'Backup time'
# Alert if newest < 24h old: $false
example.walkthrough: Add backup-age monitoring this week: the alert that fires when backups silently stop is worth more than the backup software itself.

pitfalls: Monitoring the backup server but not backup success
No offline copy — ransomware encrypts online backups first
Restore tests 'planned' for 2 years, never executed
lessons.try_it: Verify every DC has a backup newer than 24 hours.

lessons.title: Emergency Access Accounts
concepts: Two cloud-only break-glass accounts: excluded from all Conditional Access, MFA-registered, 25+ char passwords, monitored for ANY use
On-prem equivalent: sealed DSRM/DA credentials in the physical safe with quarterly testing
Usage = incident: every break-glass logon triggers immediate review — legitimate use is rare and always documented
Test quarterly: verify logon works, then rotate — an untested break-glass is Schrodinger's access

example.code:
Break-glass checklist:
  [ ] Cloud-only (not synced)
  [ ] Excluded from ALL CA policies
  [ ] MFA registered (FIDO2)
  [ ] Alert on any logon
  [ ] Tested quarterly, rotated after test
example.walkthrough: Test one break-glass account this quarter: log on, verify, rotate, document. The envelope in the safe is storage, not assurance.

pitfalls: Break-glass caught by CA policy — the lockout scenario
Never tested — discover it is broken during the emergency
No usage alerting — silent use goes unnoticed
lessons.try_it: Audit break-glass accounts against the checklist.

lessons.title: Audit Log Integrity
concepts: Attackers clear logs: protect with restricted access (no admin logon to the collector), WEF/TLS forwarding, and tamper-evident storage
Event 1102/104 (log cleared) = critical alert, always — legitimate clearing happens in change windows with records
Size and retention: balance volume against investigation needs; 90 days online minimum for AD security logs
Test the pipeline: generate a test 4625 and verify it appears in the SIEM within the SLA

example.code:
# Verify forwarding health:
# WEF: check 'ForwardedEvents' log on collector
# SIEM: search last 1h of DC security events
# Gap = broken pipeline = blind spot
example.walkthrough: Run the end-to-end test monthly: a known event on a DC must appear in the SIEM within minutes. Trust the pipeline because you test it.

pitfalls: Collector accessible to domain admins — the fox guards the evidence
No 1102 alerting — clearing goes unnoticed
Retention shorter than investigation timelines
