sections.title: Active Directory & Identity Defense — defender path

behavioral.prompt: Explain Active Directory to a non-technical executive in two minutes.
behavioral.framework: Analogy first (the company's identity phone book plus its rulebook), then why it matters (everything authenticates through it), then the risk (compromise the directory, compromise everything).
points: Plain language, no jargon pile-up
Why AD security is business security
One concrete risk the executive should fund fixing
pitfalls: Reciting FSMO roles to a CFO
No business-impact framing

behavioral.prompt: Walk me through how you would respond to a suspected DCSync attack.
behavioral.framework: Contain → investigate → eradicate → recover: isolate the suspect account, audit replication-right holders, check for golden tickets (krbtgt password changes), rotate krbtgt twice, review logs.
points: krbtgt double-rotation as the golden-ticket killer
Audit of who held replication rights
Timeline built from DC event logs
pitfalls: Only disabling the suspect account and calling it done
Forgetting that forged tickets survive a password change until krbtgt rotates twice

behavioral.prompt: A legacy application requires a service account with a weak, unchangeable password. How do you handle it?
behavioral.framework: Risk acceptance with compensating controls: isolate the account, monitor its SPN, restrict logon rights, document the exception with an expiry.
points: Never accept silently — document and time-box
Compensating controls (isolation, monitoring)
A migration plan, even a slow one
pitfalls: Just saying no with no alternative
Accepting the risk permanently with no review date

behavioral.prompt: How do you convince reluctant admins to give up standing Domain Admin?
behavioral.framework: Empathy + evidence: show the credential-theft path, offer a better workflow (just-in-time elevation, tiered accounts), pilot with volunteers.
points: Demonstrate the attack path, not just the policy
Make the secure path the easy path
Measure and report reduced exposure
pitfalls: Leading with compliance mandates
Removing access with no replacement workflow

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you found a misconfiguration before an attacker did.
behavioral.framework: STAR: how you found it (audit, alert, curiosity), the risk it posed, how you fixed it, and what you changed so it stays fixed.
points: Proactive discovery, not incident-driven
Clear risk explanation
A systemic fix, not a one-off
pitfalls: A story where someone else found it
Fixing it with no preventive follow-up

behavioral.prompt: How do you prioritize: patching domain controllers, rotating service passwords, or deploying MFA?
behavioral.framework: Risk-based ordering: what is remotely exploitable now, what enables lateral movement, what has the broadest blast radius — then sequence and explain trade-offs.
points: Explicit risk model, not gut feel
Quick wins sequenced with structural fixes
Communication of the plan to stakeholders
pitfalls: Patching everything in no particular order
Ignoring the human/organizational constraints

behavioral.prompt: Describe a disagreement about identity architecture — for example, whether to add a forest trust.
behavioral.framework: STAR: the proposal, your security analysis, how you presented the trade-off, and the decision that resulted.
points: Security analysis in business terms
Alternatives proposed (selective authentication, one-way trust)
Respect for the final decision
pitfalls: Blocking without alternatives
Security absolutism that ignores business needs

behavioral.prompt: Where is identity security heading, and how are you keeping up?
behavioral.framework: Trends (phishing-resistant MFA, tiered privilege, cloud-hybrid identity) plus a concrete learning habit.
points: Awareness of phishing-resistant authentication
Understanding of hybrid identity challenges
Active learning: labs, reading, community
pitfalls: No opinion on where the field is going
Learning only when forced by an incident

cheatsheet: Forest → trees → domains. Trust = authentication path; two-way = risk flows both ways.
FSMO: Schema Master, Domain Naming Master, PDC Emulator, RID Master, Infrastructure Master. Single-master only for operations that cannot be multi-master.
GPO = control plane: who can edit GPOs can own every machine in scope.
Kerberoasting: any user requests TGS for SPN accounts → crack offline. Defense: long random passwords, managed service accounts, monitor TGS requests.
AS-REP roasting: pre-auth disabled → anonymous crackable response. Fix: re-enable pre-auth (default), rotate password.
Pass-the-hash/ticket: reuse stolen credential material without the password. Defense: Credential Guard, tiering, no credential reuse across tiers.
DCSync: replication rights abused to pull hashes. Audit 'Replicating Directory Changes All' holders; treat surprises as incidents.
Tiered model: Tier 0 creds never touch Tier 1/2 systems. LAPS: unique local admin password per machine. MFA: phishing-resistant (FIDO2) for privileged accounts.

glossary.def: The AD security boundary: one or more domain trees sharing schema and configuration. Compromise of the forest root compromises everything inside.
An authentication relationship between domains or forests; defines whose authentication decisions are honored.
Flexible Single Master Operations: five AD roles held by single DCs for operations that cannot run multi-master.
Service Principal Name: the Kerberos identifier for a service; accounts holding SPNs are Kerberoasting targets.
Requesting crackable Kerberos service tickets (TGS) for SPN accounts as any user, then cracking them offline.
Exploiting accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled to obtain crackable responses without credentials.
Authenticating with a stolen password hash instead of the plaintext password.
Authenticating with a stolen Kerberos ticket, bypassing password authentication entirely.
Abusing domain replication rights to pull password hashes from a DC while impersonating another DC.
Registering a rogue DC to inject malicious replication changes into AD.
Separating privileged accounts into tiers (0: identity systems, 1: servers, 2: workstations) so credentials never cross tiers.
Local Administrator Password Solution: unique, rotating local admin passwords per machine.
Windows virtualization-based isolation of credential material so stolen hashes/tickets are harder to extract.
A forged Kerberos ticket-granting ticket using the krbtgt hash; killed by rotating krbtgt twice.

simulations.title: DCSync replication attack in progress
simulations.brief: The SIEM fires at 02:14: a non-domain-controller host is issuing DRS replication requests against DC02. Credential theft is underway right now. Work the response.

steps.symptom: Event 4662 audit shows Ds-Replication-Get-Changes rights exercised by SVC-backup from WS-114, which is not a domain controller.
options: DCSync attack: a compromised account with replication rights is pulling password hashes — treat as active credential theft
Normal backup traffic: the backup service legitimately replicates the directory
A misconfigured monitoring agent polling LDAP
Routine SYSVOL replication between domain controllers
evidence: 02:14:03 Event 4662 — Subject: SVC-backup — Object: DC=corp,DC=local — Accesses: DS-Replication-Get-Changes, DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All — Source host: WS-114
WS-114: finance workstation. Domain controllers: DC01, DC02 only. SVC-backup: backup service account, member of no replication-authorized group per policy.
steps.explain: Only domain controllers should issue DRS replication calls. A workstation exercising DS-Replication-Get-Changes is the textbook DCSync pattern — it pulls every password hash in the domain, including krbtgt.

steps.symptom: You must contain the attack without tipping off the intruder's persistence. What is the correct containment order?
options: Reset the krbtgt password first, then investigate
Isolate WS-114 from the network, disable SVC-backup, then hunt for additional footholds before any password resets
Delete the SVC-backup account immediately
Shut down DC02 to stop the replication
evidence: Containment: sever attacker access first (host isolation, account disable), THEN remediate credentials. Resetting krbtgt while the attacker still holds access lets them re-establish.
WS-114: active C2 beacon to 185.220.x.x every 60s.
steps.explain: Isolation plus account disable cuts the attacker's hands off first. Password resets come after you confirm the foothold is gone, or the attacker just re-steals the new hashes.

steps.symptom: WS-114 is isolated and SVC-backup disabled. The attacker held DCSync rights for ~40 minutes. What completes eradication?
options: Re-enable SVC-backup with a new password
Reset the krbtgt account password twice, force password resets for all privileged accounts, audit replication rights
Restore DC02 from last night's backup
Block port 445 on the firewall
evidence: Memory capture from WS-114 shows Mimikatz sekurlsa output. DCSync window: 01:34–02:14. Hashes for 1,900+ accounts exfiltrated, including krbtgt.
After krbtgt compromise: reset twice to invalidate both current and previous password (ticket lifetime overlap). Audit all principals with DS-Replication-Get-Changes.
steps.explain: With hashes exfiltrated, every derived ticket is suspect. The double krbtgt reset invalidates old and new ticket-granting tickets; privileged resets and a replication-rights audit close the loop.

simulations.debrief: DCSync turns any account with replication rights into a domain-wide password dump. Respond in order: confirm the anomaly, isolate the host and disable the account, hunt for footholds, then double-reset krbtgt and audit who holds replication rights. Prevention is least privilege on the directory itself.

simulations.title: Kerberoasting: hunting crackable service tickets
simulations.brief: Overnight the SIEM logged a burst of Kerberos TGS-REQ messages with RC4 encryption from a single workstation. A service account may be getting roasted. Investigate.

steps.symptom: 3,100 TGS requests in 20 minutes from WS-087, all requesting RC4-encrypted service tickets.
options: Likely Kerberoasting: bulk TGS requests for RC4 tickets are harvested for offline cracking
Normal service startup after a reboot
A backup job enumerating shares
DNS misconfiguration causing ticket retries
evidence: 00:41–01:02: 3,104 TGS-REQ from 10.4.8.87 (WS-087), etype rc4-hmac. No failures — valid user context.
Normal TGS rate per host: ~40/hour. RC4 usage fleet-wide: <1% of tickets.
steps.explain: Kerberoasting needs no privilege: any authenticated user can request service tickets and crack them offline. The volume plus forced RC4 downgrade is the signature — legitimate clients overwhelmingly negotiate AES.

steps.symptom: The tickets target MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local. What do you check next to confirm the exposure?
options: The service account's password age, complexity, and whether it is a managed service account
The SQL server's patch level
The workstation's antivirus status
The domain functional level
evidence: SVC-sql: password last set 2019-03-11 (7 years). Not a gMSA. Member of Domain Admins (legacy).
steps.explain: Kerberoasting succeeds against weak service-account passwords. A seven-year-old password on a Domain Admin service account is the jackpot: crack the ticket, own the domain.

steps.symptom: Confirmed: SVC-sql is roastable and over-privileged. What is the durable fix?
options: Disable Kerberos on the SQL server
Migrate to a group Managed Service Account with a long random password, remove Domain Admin, enforce AES
Rename the service account
Block RC4 at the firewall
evidence: gMSA: 240-char auto-rotated passwords, cannot be cracked offline practically. AES-only: removes the RC4 downgrade path. Least privilege: service accounts are never Domain Admins.
steps.explain: gMSAs remove the crackable secret entirely through automatic rotation of very long passwords, and AES-only kills the downgrade. Renaming changes nothing about the hash.

simulations.debrief: Kerberoasting is a defender's audit gift: it only works where service accounts are weak. Hunt for TGS volume anomalies, then fix the root cause — managed service accounts, long random passwords, AES enforcement, and least privilege.

simulations.title: Forged Kerberos tickets bypassing authentication
simulations.brief: A user account shows successful logons to servers it never touched, with ticket lifetimes of 10 years. Something is forging Kerberos tickets. Track it down.

steps.symptom: TGT lifetime 10 years for user j.chen; logons to FILE03 and BACKUP01 with no corresponding interactive session.
options: Golden ticket: forged TGTs signed with the stolen krbtgt hash, valid for years and invisible to normal logon auditing
A misconfigured SSO token cache
Clock skew between the workstation and the DC
Cached credentials from an old VPN session
evidence: TGT issued for j.chen with lifetime 87600h. Domain policy max: 10h. No 4768 (TGT request) precedes the 4769 service tickets.
No logon session for j.chen on FILE03 in EDR telemetry — the tickets arrive without authentication.
steps.explain: Golden tickets are minted offline with the krbtgt hash, so the KDC never logs a TGT request. Absurd lifetimes and logons with no authentication event are the tells.

steps.symptom: You suspect krbtgt compromise. How do you confirm the scope before remediating?
options: Check every host for malware
Correlate anomalous-lifetime tickets across DCs, identify when the krbtgt hash was first abused, and inventory accounts with replication rights
Force a password change for j.chen
Rebuild the affected file servers
evidence: Anomalous-lifetime TGTs seen on DC01 and DC02 since 2026-09-19. First abuse predates the j.chen sightings by three weeks.
Principals with DS-Replication-Get-Changes: Domain Controllers, SVC-backup, SVC-oldmigrator.
steps.explain: Scope first: the earliest forged ticket bounds the compromise window, and the replication-rights inventory shows every path the attacker could have taken to steal krbtgt.

steps.symptom: Scope confirmed: krbtgt hash stolen via the stale SVC-oldmigrator account. What is the remediation sequence?
options: Disable SVC-oldmigrator, reset krbtgt twice, reset all privileged passwords, remove stale replication rights
Reset krbtgt once and monitor
Demote and rebuild both DCs
Enable MFA on the VPN
evidence: krbtgt double-reset: two resets invalidate tickets minted under both the current and previous hash. Single reset leaves the previous-hash window open.
steps.explain: Kill the entry path, double-reset krbtgt to burn both ticket generations, rotate everything the stolen hash could have touched, and remove the stale rights so it cannot recur.

simulations.debrief: Golden tickets persist because defenders reset once or never. The discipline is: scope the abuse window, kill the theft path, double-reset krbtgt, rotate privileged credentials, and audit replication rights so the theft cannot repeat.

simulations.title: The legacy app that demands Domain Admin
simulations.brief: A vendor's legacy inventory app requires its service account to be a Domain Admin or it will not start. The business says it is critical. Decide the identity architecture.

steps.symptom: Vendor support insists: 'SVC-inventory must be Domain Admin. No workaround.' The app runs on one member server.
options: Grant Domain Admin — the business need outweighs the risk
Refuse outright and let the app stay broken
Profile the app's actual needs with auditing, grant only the specific rights it uses, isolate the server in a tier-appropriate OU with constrained delegation
Make it a local admin on the domain controller
evidence: Vendor requires 'Domain Admin or equivalent' — undocumented which privileges are actually exercised.
Tier 0 (domain controllers, identity systems): only Tier 0 admin accounts. Member servers: Tier 1. Workstations: Tier 2. No account crosses tiers.
steps.explain: Vendors ask for Domain Admin because it is easy, not because it is needed. Auditing reveals the true minimum — usually a handful of specific rights — and the tier model keeps those rights from reaching Tier 0.

steps.symptom: Auditing shows the app only writes to one OU and reads three attributes. The vendor still refuses to support a non-DA configuration. Your call?
options: Document the exact delegated rights, implement them, accept the support risk with business sign-off, and monitor the account as privileged
Give up and grant Domain Admin
Run the app on a domain controller so DA is 'contained'
Create a second Domain Admin as a backup
evidence: Residual risk: unsupported config. Mitigations: delegated rights documented, account monitored as Tier 1 privileged, server isolated, quarterly re-audit.
steps.explain: Security decisions are risk decisions with owners. Delegation plus monitoring plus documented business acceptance beats both blanket refusal (business harm) and surrender (domain-wide risk).

simulations.debrief: Standing Domain Admin for applications is how domains fall. Profile the real need, delegate precisely, enforce the tier boundary, and make the residual risk explicit and owned — never silent.

simulations.title: AdFind-style reconnaissance at 3 AM
simulations.brief: DC01 logs show thousands of LDAP queries enumerating group memberships and trust relationships from a helpdesk workstation at 03:00. Nobody works the helpdesk at 3 AM. Hunt it.

steps.symptom: 4,200 LDAP queries in 35 minutes from HD-022, enumerating 'Domain Admins', trusts, and GPOs. Source user: helpdesk intern account.
options: Active Directory reconnaissance: pre-attack enumeration mapping privileged groups, trusts, and policy — likely AdFind or similar tooling
The intern doing diligent after-hours study
A vulnerability scanner's scheduled run
Replication traffic misattributed to the workstation
evidence: 03:02–03:37: 4,213 queries from 10.4.9.22. Filters: (memberOf=CN=Domain Admins*), (objectClass=trustedDomain), (objectClass=groupPolicyContainer). Base DN: whole domain.
adfind.exe executed 03:01 from C:\Users\intern\Downloads. Parent: cmd.exe. No ticket for after-hours work.
steps.explain: Bulk enumeration of privileged groups, trusts, and GPOs with a dedicated recon binary is the attack-planning phase. Legitimate admin work is targeted; this is cartography.

steps.symptom: Recon confirmed on HD-022. What is the right next move?
options: Confront the intern immediately
Isolate HD-022, preserve memory and disk for forensics, reset the intern account credentials, and hunt for follow-on activity (lateral movement, persistence)
Delete adfind.exe and close the ticket
Block LDAP at the firewall
evidence: Recon is the precursor, not the payload. Assume the account is compromised until proven otherwise; hunt for what the recon was planning.
steps.explain: Recon means an attack is being planned — possibly by the account owner, possibly by someone who stole the session. Preserve evidence, kill the access, and hunt for the next phase instead of just deleting the tool.

simulations.debrief: LDAP recon is the attacker's map-making. Baseline normal query volumes, alert on bulk enumeration of privileged objects, and treat recon as the start of an investigation — not the end of one.

consoleSims.title: Work the DCSync SIEM alert
consoleSims.brief: Alert ALT-2077: 'DCSync replication from non-DC host WS-114'. Acknowledge it, assign it to the identity analyst, and escalate it to Tier 2.

tasks.hint: Click acknowledge on alert ALT-2077 in the SIEM queue.
Use the assign control on ALT-2077 and enter analyst r.okafor.
Click escalate on ALT-2077 to send it to Tier 2.

consoleSims.debrief: Identity-plane alerts are never low priority: acknowledge so nobody else duplicates the work, assign a named owner, escalate with the DCSync context attached.

consoleSims.title: Open the identity incident ticket
consoleSims.brief: Open a P1 incident ticket for the DCSync attack, assign it to the on-call identity responder, and move it to in-progress.

tasks.instruction: Create a P1 ticket titled 'DCSync attack from WS-114'.
tasks.hint: Create a ticket with title 'DCSync attack from WS-114' and priority P1.

consoleSims.debrief: Active credential theft gets a P1, a named owner, and a live status — the ticket is the shared picture while the response runs.

consoleSims.title: Cut off the rogue replication host
consoleSims.brief: WS-114 (10.4.8.114) is pulling directory replication traffic. Drop its SMB/replication traffic at the host firewall, then set the FORWARD chain default to DROP.

tasks.instruction: Add a rule dropping TCP port 445 from 10.4.8.114 on INPUT.
tasks.hint: Add an INPUT rule: protocol tcp, port 445, source 10.4.8.114, action DROP.

tasks.instruction: Set the FORWARD chain default policy to DROP.
tasks.hint: Set the default policy of the FORWARD chain to DROP.

consoleSims.debrief: Network containment buys time: drop the attacker's replication and C2 paths at the firewall while the host is isolated and credentials are rotated.

consoleSims.title: Lock down the offline AD backup
consoleSims.brief: The offline NTDS backup at /backups/ntds.dit is world-readable. Restrict it to root-only access.

tasks.instruction: Change the owner of /backups/ntds.dit to root.

consoleSims.debrief: An offline NTDS.dit is the whole domain in a file. World-readable backups are a DCSync without the network — permissions are a control, not paperwork.

terminalMissions.title: Find the recon queries
terminalMissions.brief: Search the LDAP query log for bulk enumeration of the Domain Admins group.
terminalMissions.success_message: Recon queries located — bulk enumeration of Domain Admins confirmed.

terminalMissions.title: Verify the AD backup integrity
terminalMissions.brief: Before restoring anything, verify the offline NTDS backup hash matches the known-good value.
objectives: Run sha256sum on ntds-backup.dit and confirm the filename in the output
terminalMissions.success_message: Backup hash verified — the offline copy is intact.

terminalMissions.title: Check domain controller SRV records
terminalMissions.brief: Confirm DNS still advertises the legitimate domain controllers via SRV lookup.
objectives: Dig the _ldap._tcp SRV record for the domain
terminalMissions.success_message: SRV records resolve to the legitimate domain controllers.

terminalMissions.title: Hunt SYSVOL for planted scripts
terminalMissions.brief: Attackers plant scripts in SYSVOL for GPO-based persistence. Find any PowerShell scripts there.
terminalMissions.success_message: SYSVOL sweep complete — planted scripts identified for review.

terminalMissions.title: Diff the Group Policy backup
terminalMissions.brief: Compare the known-good GPO export against the current one to spot unauthorized changes.
terminalMissions.success_message: Policy drift found — unauthorized GPO changes are now visible.

terminalMissions.title: Sort the failed logon list
terminalMissions.brief: Sort failed-logons.txt so you can spot the accounts under password-spray attack.
terminalMissions.success_message: Logons sorted — spray targets clustered for the hunt.

terminalMissions.title: Count the replication events
terminalMissions.brief: Count how many DRS replication events fired during the attack window.
objectives: Count lines in drs-events.log with wc
terminalMissions.success_message: Event count captured — the replication window is now quantified.
